#6626. Vintage Watch Experts Break Down Their 6 Favorite Timepieces

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

And another thing, a watch collector might say as they try to sell you on the virtues of the hobby, is that you can bring them anywhere. Unlike other high-value collectibles—cars or paintings, say—you can wear even the rarest of grail-worthy timepieces to, say, a dimly lit bar. Which is precisely where James Fisk—the photographer behind the images in the just-released Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide, written by the renowned dealers Eric Wind and Charlie Dunne—encountered one of the most historic tickers in the book.

Last September, Fisk was at the Waldorf Astoria in New York when he spotted a collector wearing the coveted 1940s Longines model known as the “Tre Tacche.” Watches are challenging subjects even in a photo studio, but Fisk was forced to stumble around the hotel bar looking for any slice of decent lighting to capture the Longines before it slipped through his fingers forever. Used to working on the fly, the photographer keeps 40 or so fabric swatches with him at all times, just in case he needs to lay a watch on top of one as a backdrop for an impromptu shoot.

“You meet someone who just happens to be wearing something really special on the wrist that day, and you have to just be ready for it,” Fisk tells me. It’s how many of the legendary vintage watches—mildly important subjects for a book on the topic—ended up in Wind and Dunne’s new tome.

The book is a comprehensive deep dive into the booming world of vintage watch collecting. Wind and Dunne take readers on a Jungle Cruise-style tour of this sometimes daunting hobby: On your left are the questions that all newcomers should know to ask before buying a vintage watch; on your right, you’ll find testimonies from famous collectors like David Chang, Ronny Chieng, and Daniel Dae Kim; straight ahead are dispatches on the most important brands, from Rolex to Piaget.

Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide is designed to be as welcoming and accessible as possible. While many watch volumes sell for hundreds of dollars, Dunne and Wind made it a point to price theirs at $60 (or $50 on Amazon right now). “A lot of people will be able to afford this book,” Dunne says. “And then, hopefully, they’ll aspire to get some of the watches in it and it’ll ignite their interest in the hobby.”

Below are Wind and Dunne’s favorite selections from the book, including one that the latter was most insistent on including to represent the more affordable side of the spectrum.

There may be two six-figure watches on the cover, but flip just a few pages into the book and you’ll find this delightful little example from Fortis. “I forced Eric to put that in,” Dunne jokes. “He said, ‘We're not putting that in—it's too cheap!” The watch sells for just a touch over $1,000, and this exact piece was in Wind’s collection for several years. He calls it a personal favorite from his years of collecting.

The Shipman might not be historically important or carry great provenance, but it serves an important dimension in the book as a representative for the many types of pieces that comprise a true collection. “Not only [does it show] the range of what is out there as far as exceptional watches at all price points, but also it's one of the most fun and quirky watches in the book,” Dunne says. “You want to have very, very serious watches in your collection, but you also want to have things that put a smile on your face at any price point.”

How do you choose the cover stars for a book about vintage watches? You start with the obvious: The Rolex “Paul Newman” Daytona (bottom) is the poster boy for vintage collecting. The famed Phillips auctioneer Aurel Bacs, who sold the actor’s personal version for a record $17.8 million, calls Newman wearing this special variant “the Adam and Eve moment in Rolex collecting.”

But the Daytona’s partner on the cover, the Audemars Piguet ref. 5516, is an unexpected choice that packs just as much historical heft. “This is one of the most important watches ever made, because of the leap year indicator” Wind says. “AP beat Patek by over 20 years to have a leap year indicator on the bottom. This and the Royal Oak are probably two of the greatest impacts on the Swiss watch industry.” Only nine were made, and Wind sold this example for $545,000 while he was at Christie’s in 2015. I love the specificity of the watch’s leap-year function, which only comes into play once every four years.

Wind and Dunne are longtime evangelists for the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch in the late ’40s and early ’50s. This particular reference is modified to include a tide indicator at the 9 o’clock subdial, done up in extremely pretty tones of sandy tan and deep sea blue. The example featured in the book remains pristine—with a perfect eggshell-white dial—thanks to the original owner stuffing it in a drawer unworn for decades. The watch got to Wind by way of a friend, whom he sent to fetch it from a diner in the original owner’s home state of Arizona.

The watch that Fisk scrambled to shoot in a hotel bar was well worth the hustle. “Longines, in some sense, was Rolex before Rolex,” Wind says. The brand was “the tool watch manufacturer in the 1930s and 1940s, particularly with their Tre Tacche cases. Many of the great aviators and pioneers of the time wore Longines watches.” The model gets its nickname from the three notches on the caseback that helped watchmakers screw the case together tighter to prevent water and dust from getting inside.

This is a classic watch—a defining example of a dress model—done up with a particularly sleek dial. Patek Philippe made endless examples of the 96, allowing collectors to select their favorite flavor from the lot. Wind and Dunne sold this example but both wish they could have it back. “ I don't think it's coming to the light ever,” Dunne laments.

To capture the glossy black dial in the book, Fisk shot the watch at two different angles to mimic the experience of tilting it back and forth in your hands.

The very last watch added to the book was this version of the GMT-Master, one of the Crown’s most important models. The ref. 1675 isn’t the first GMT-Master that Rolex made, but it’s considered the platonic ideal visually and the most collectible among vintage watch lovers. Its predecessors featured troublesome bezels that were prone to cracking, as well as poisonous amounts of radium.

The 1675 was produced for just over 20 years, from 1959 to 1980. This one belongs to Fisk and was on his wrist when we met last week. “We got this right as the pages were printed,” Dunne says, “and we started yelling in emails [to the publisher] saying, ‘We have to stop everything. Put this page in there.’”

#6624. Ciara Has One Holiday Cooking Rule & You Really Don't Want To Break It

She's all for getting creative with Oreos, although she has much stronger feelings about the rest of the menu.

Ciara has one request for whoever’s in charge of Christmas dinner: Please, whatever you do, make sure you’re up for the assignment. She’s willing to embrace a little holiday mess, but apparently, there’s a limit to how far that generosity extends into the kitchen.

“All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”

Ciara, a mom of four, certainly understands how quickly the festivities can get away from you. “Christmas in our house is full of love, excitement and a little chaos,” she said in a statement. But when it comes to the actual Christmas menu, she’s got some traditions she’s pretty attached to, many of which go all the way back to her childhood in Atlanta, Georgia.

"If you know one thing about us ATLians, you have Thanksgiving on Christmas. The same meal comes back around again," she told Delish.

And we’re talking a serious Southern spread: turkey legs, mac and cheese, candied yams, collard greens, chitlins, and pig feet. She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara says those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

#6623. Every David Fincher Killer, Definitively Ranked

David Fincher is a rare breed of chameleonic auteur. In the past 40 years, he's directed music videos, commercials, feature films, and television series, all of which keep garnering more cultural importance, either immediately or in retrospect (hey, look, David Fincher directed a 1987 video for a single from a random Philly bar rock band!) Fincher is known for his technical prowess, his “impossible eye,” and his pioneering mastery of digital technology. He’s made love letters to old Hollywood, ripped-from-the-headlines tech-industry autopsies that render depositions as white-knuckle suspense, and popcorn home-invasion flicks. He’s taken turns at IP-franchise stewardship, adapted bestselling airport paperbacks, and told the oddly touching story of a mild-mannered, even-tempered gentleman from New Orleans who ages backwards. But if Fincher has a career throughline, a raison d’etre, it’s his pursuit and depiction of killers—a focus made quite overt in The Killer, a fascinating and highly meta film which hits Netflix Friday after a limited theatrical run over the past two weeks.

In Fincher's films, killers—particularly serial killers—provide an extreme window into human nature. They are symptoms of a sick society, prophets, self-appointed Gods and monsters, blank canvases for us to project our conspiracies and insecurities onto, or would-be celebrities killing for attention from a sensation-hungry media that's all too happy to give it to them. In the pale light of day or the fluorescent light of a prison visiting area, they're often sad, awkward misfits who understand themselves and their actions even less than we do. But by necessity, they're also methodical people who must put a great deal of thought and care into their grisly work in order to continue working. In this way, Fincher sees them as the equivalent of process-mad directors, blocking their victims and staging their crime scenes before selling them to a confused but riveted public.

Time and time again, across his filmography, the image most associated with Fincher is the killer— or the hapless detectives pursuing them—shot from below, almost swallowed whole by a monochromatic backdrop that looms both far above and far behind them, dimly but immaculately lit, and bathed in shadow, inside Fincher's uncommonly steady, all-seeing and all-knowing frame. The killer’s maniacal focus, their certitude, is ours. The detective’s confusion—their understanding that they’re a step behind and a beat late, that they will never get the satisfying answers, the closure they’re looking for—is ours, too.

So for art, and for fun, let’s evaluate the many killers who've made Fincher's body of work as incredible and indelible as it is, based on a shifting, subjective equation of quality, efficacy, body count, and how they’re represented by the auteur himself.

Fight Club is a satire about bereft ineffectual masculinity, about neutered men crushed under Ikea catalogs, about eighth-grade-boy-level rebellion against materialism, capitalism, and every societal convention that places value on anything except chiseled abs, skinned knuckles, bullshit patter, and rugged individualism.

The “kill” here is committed by Edward Norton, as a character identified in the credits as “The Narrator” who murders Tyler Durden—his child, his liberator, his tormentor, and his imaginary friend—by, uh, shooting the side of his mouth, sort of? Somehow, the famously meticulous Fincher lands on a resolution that makes absolutely no sense according to the laws of physical interaction between The Narrator and Tyler Durden established within the rest of the film. Why does this apparition, who knows everything the narrator knows, and can punch The Narrator, can harm him physically without receiving the impact of those assaults, and can’t even be hit by The Narrator, die with his brains blown out as a result of his alter ego shooting off a chunk of his jaw? This is, hands down, the worst “kill” in the Fincher filmography.

22. The Random Guy Who Kills Madonna, “Bad Girl” (1993)

Fincher did his most important music video work for his muse and rumored paramour Madonna, who tapped him to direct videos for hits like “Vogue” and “Express Yourself.” But one of their less heralded collaborations was this bizarre minor work, a video (for a song from Erotica) that plays like a dumbed-down Wings of Desire. Madonna is a stressed-out high-achieving corporate type who unwinds by making bad and eventually fatal decisions. After her Bruno Ganz-like guardian angel (Christopher Walken) makes out with her, she pursues sex with a hookup who clearly intends to murder her. We only see the killer from Madonna's POV, and when he kills her it's presented as her choice, rather than the result of any kind of premeditated plot by the killer; he's more of a prop than a person.

21. Weyland-Yutani Employee, Alien3 (1992)

For a filmmaker who so regularly trades in death, Fincher has depicted shockingly few frivolous ones. Nearly every kill in his work is personal and meaningful. But this is an exception. Towards the end of Alien3 , a commando representing the wantonly evil corporation smokes Francis Aaron, one of the COs on the prison planet Ripley has crash-landed on. The scene underscores the cynical ruthlessness of the outfit, but ultimately it’s just a faceless grunt shooting a stranger.

20. The Security Guard, Fight Club (1999)

In the act of executing Operation Latte Thunder, an ingenious plan to weaponize a piece of corporate art mounted in an office park fountain to destroy a franchise coffee shop in the lobby of a nearby building, Robert Paulson (Meatloaf) is murdered by an extremely extra security guard, who shoots him in the head as he flees the scene of the crime. It’s another somewhat frivolous murder, but the fallout tells us a lot about Tyler Durden’s cult of personality and its effect on its dumbass followers.

19. Frank Underwood, House of Cards (2013-2018)

There are several killers from this groundbreaking, trashy Netflix politico soap you won’t see on this list. This is because the totality of Fincher’s involvement is unclear—he may have imprinted his filmic language on the entirety of the show's run, but he only directed the first two episodes (unlike Mindhunter, his second effort with Netflix, on which he directed seven of 19 episodes across two seasons.) But in the House of Cards pilot, in order to show us just what kind of devious, deliciously shitty archvillain Kevin Spacey's Francis Underwood is going to be, he gleefully, flagrantly bucks the old screenwriting maxim “Don't kill the dog”—and not for the first time—by having Frank strangle his pooch, which has been hit by a car.

The heroine of Aerosmith’s outlier conscious anthem reclaims her narrative by killing her rapist father. It’s an odd “message” song and an odd video, but both were groundbreaking and transgressive at the time. It’s a completely justified revenge killing that Fincher had to sell through suggestion to get played on MTV.

17. Lisbeth Salander, The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo (2011)

Lisbeth (Rooney Mara) slaps the shit out of Martin Vanger (Stellan Skarsgård) with a long iron, then chases him down on her motorcycle as he attempts to flee in a Range Rover, causing him to crash and burn. When she cocks a gun and asks Daniel Craig’s Mikael Blomkvist, “May I kill him?” before lighting out after Vanger, devoid of emotion, it’s the most badass moment of a very badass film.

Bald Sigourney Weaver kills the “Runner” xenomorph by setting off sprinklers after it jumps out of a river of molten lead, causing it to explode. Then—rather than allowing The Corporation to take a parasite chestburster out of her and potentially spare her life—she swan-dives backwards into the lead, killing herself and taking the alien with her—a sci-fi Joan of Arc.

15. Gottfried and Martin Vanger, The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo (2011)

Playing the role of a sicko pervert hiding in plain sight is a stretch for Skarsgård; Martin Vanger is a second-generation killer who shits on his dad for putting up rookie numbers and has a whole secret sex dungeon in his basement where he’s presumably killed dozens of women. Sadly, we must deduct points because Martin ends up dying as a result of overlong monologuing, like a 70s Bond villain.

14. (Tie) Monte Rissell, Rose Barnwright/Frank Janderman/Benjamin Barnwright, Jerry Brudos, Dennis Rader, Richard Speck, Darrell Gene Devier, David Berkowitz, William Pierce Jr., William Henry Hance, Elmer Wayne Henley Jr., Charles “Tex” Watson, Charles Manson*, Paul Bateson, Wayne Bertram Williams, Mindhunter (2017-2019)

David Fincher’s great Netflix series, a history of the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, takes place mainly in the aftermath of its serial-killer subjects' various sprees, so we see few dead bodies onscreen. But as it turns out, talking to killers in quiet rooms and delving into their psyches is just as sensational and disturbing as the graphically depicted comic-book corpses in Se7en. The show is two Feds tearing the cover off America and discovering a teeming morass of perverts beneath the floorboards, up to their necks in muck. What we discover—in this crucial chapter of what feels like a career-long attempt by Fincher to unmake Se7en and its godlike antagonist—is that a lot of these killers are dull, impulsive, mentally-ill misfits and outcasts.

“To support devices," cheers Herman Mankiewicz, after delivering the first draft of his masterpiece, Citizen Kane. In the biopic written by Fincher’s father, booze is the fuel that allows the screenwriter to write, but kills his career one painful, impolitic-outburst-filled social interaction at a time, before it finally kills him, too. Alcohol is the lubricant that powers Mank’s genius, even as it obfuscates that genius and speeds his demise. The bottle both makes him and unmakes him, like Popeye if spinach destroyed his liver. It’s a self-inflicted slow killer, which makes its work all the more painful and tragic to witness.

12. (Tie) Raoul & Burnham, Panic Room (2002)

In Fincher’s masterful and inventive “conventional” thriller, Raoul (Dwight Yoakam) domes spoiled, insufferable, cornrowed Junior (Jared Leto) when he tries to walk away from the robbery they're pulling. Later, Burnham (Forest Whittaker) sacrifices himself and $22 million in bearer bonds to kill Raoul and save the day. Hard to say which is more satisfying.

11. Tobacco, American Cancer Society Commercial (1985)

The Big Bang of Fincher’s career, when he transitioned from Industrial Light & Magic cameraman and matte photographer to auteur. His first effort was this commercial, made for just $7,000, which several television stations banned because it was too graphic and disturbing. We have to side with the networks on this one—it’s a truly horrifying ad, a nightmare vision of the Starchild puppet from 2001 as a fetus double-fisting darts in the womb. But it’s an impressive work of visceral agitprop, one that had the potential to reconfigure the way we thought about this deadly but fairly common behavior in the 80s.

In Fincher’s latest, Michael Fassbender plays the unnamed, titular assassin in a procedural that’s all process. He's a classic Fincher protagonist, a type-A creature of habit and ritual. The wrinkle is he kind of sucks at his job—or at least, when we meet him, has reached a point where he’s no longer able to execute his work according to the dispassionate code he lives and works by.

So, yes, he’s obviously baited into killing John Doe, and basically gets his wife killed by being an idiot and giving his name to her killer in an angry impulsive rush when John Doe is right next to him pretending to be a nosy reporter, and by giving into his emotions and impulses he’s throwing his life and his career away—but Mills ranks this high because of Pitt's incredible work in the tortured moments before Mills fulfills John Doe's master plan. It's an all-time great performance that's seared into your brain forever after you've watched it once.

8. The Verdusco Brothers, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

Matt Groove and JB Tadena play Eddie and Fernando Verdusco, the gangster antagonists that walked directly out of Quentin Tarantino’s cinema-fried brain and into Fincher’s latest. The film has been sold as a play on a chatty Elmore Leonard crime story, but with touches like the Verduscos, it’s more like a muddy puddle of all different stripes of exploitation film, from noir to horror to splatter. The Verduscos are Filipino but present as Yakuza hitmen, with a dash of Mortal Kombat cartoonishness. It’s easy to give characters badass motherfucker names that insist upon themselves, with writers and directors who simply expect us to find them scary and cool with little to no proof besides a slow-mo entrance and a needle drop. But Tarantino and Fincher earn the mythology with a particularly terrifying and gnarly introductory home invasion murder (invoking Panic Room) of a family of four. Esmeralda, the rhino-killing war hammer brandished by Fernando, has the instant iconographic “weapon as characterization” power of which Tarantino’s longtime friend and collaborator Robert Rodriguez would be envious.

Alien3 is Fincher’s canon event; the formatively traumatic experience of tangling with a cynical studio on his first feature made him the director he became. Having the film taken away from him taught Fincher the importance of demanding complete creative control. So it’s either ironic or brilliant that in many ways, this Xenomorph is a metaphor for the director, an alien antagonist (with the characteristics of a rabid dog!) resisting a sinister corporation that wants to cage and exploit him for its own evil purposes.

6. Time, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008)

In a movie about a guy born as an old man who ages in reverse, a byproduct of his disease is Benjamin (Brad Pitt) must “blend in”, experiencing his childhood in an old folks home where death is routine. Benjamin Button lives outside of time, breaks the rules of time, and in the process explains the ravages of time. Throughout the film we watch everyone around Benjamin die: From war, from old age, from disease, and finally, from being born in reverse. It contains the most stunning and heartbreaking kills in Fincher’s filmography because they are not a product of a sicko's grand design, but simply nature taking its course, harrowing in its obvious, matter of fact inevitability.

The breakout star of Mindhunter, Edmund Kemper was the Co-Ed Killer—a hulking monster who killed many people and occasionally had sex with his victims' decapitated heads—and in the show, he’s the catalyst for the birth of the behavioral science unit. Cameron Britton plays Kemper as a verbose, precise, calmly menacing giant with thick frames and a trim mustache. He’s the most Fincheresque antagonist in the series. Kemper is lucid and clear-eyed, incisive, articulate, and occasionally even funny. Understanding what he’s done—and exactly why and how he did it— is critical to the protagonists' mission, and Kemper understands this, which makes him that much more terrifying.

Another meticulous, disciplined Fincher avatar who has checked every box and arranged for every contingency. Amazing Amy is a feminist archvillain exploiting misogyny to liberate herself from the American prison of marriage and the cool-girl wife’s role therein. She’s a deeply petty scorned woman of iron will, expert at manipulating the public, the authorities, staged crime scenes, and her husband.

3. Cliff Booth, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

In their fourth film together, Fincher and Pitt unlock their greatest character, which is doubly impressive when you consider that, the first time we met Booth, it earned Pitt his long-awaited Oscar. This version of Cliff Booth, nearly a decade older and mostly washed, is a more interesting character and one of Fincher’s greatest killers because he unlocks a darkness that is only hinted at in Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. In that film, Cliff is an affable and doggedly loyal sidekick. When he kills (on screen), it’s self-defense, protecting his buddy from harm, and you can squint and think, “This just might be a roughneck, badass dude with a heart of gold.” In this installment, Cliff operates according to his personal moral compass, which in some cases involves premeditated, entirely avoidable, cold-blooded murder. He’s observing a uniquely American form of zen, existing in an overloaded sensory flow state on a spectrum that encompasses all manner of kinetic pleasure, remaining at ease and even-keeled whether he is bartending, Demolition Derby driving, getting slapped by a Goddess with frying pan hands, running a film projector at the New Bev, clutching an Old Chattanooga, or, of course, killing.

The film, and the killer, that has in many ways defined Fincher. Speaking to Esquire, before releasing Zodiac, the director said, “I don’t want to make a film serial killers masturbate to.” The line was an obvious dig at his own second feature, which is pure serial-killer porn and would set the template countless lesser movies would aspire to going forward. John Doe is a true mastermind who executes creative, horrific, gimmicky murders inspired by the Bible's deadly sins. But most importantly, he’s always a step ahead, always smarter than the cops coming after him, and his win at the end is absolute. Morgan Freeman’s terrified exclamation at the film's climax sums up the plot of the whole film: “John Doe has the upper hand!”

In Fincher’s masterpiece of form and statement, he’s at the height of his powers, revisiting the serial killer as a “celebrated” cultural figure and a malignant expression of society, and what he comes back with is maddening emptiness. Instead of a running inner monologue, we’re given nothing—not even the killer's identity (or identities.) The first half is a painstakingly made and researched film, scrubbed of all romance and sentimentality, that comes as close as fiction can to mimicking the endless, mundane texture of reality. Then, the killer dissolves.

To Fincher, the Zodiac Killer isn't a person, but an idea, an unanswered question, an unresolvable puzzle. Although different actors show up playing people who might be the culprit, the Zodiac haunts the film mostly as an absent menace. Conflicting motivations and theories are thrown at the viewer and it’s impossible to sift what circumstantial evidence is real from bullshit. Some characters favor one suspect, some another, nothing ever adds up, and no one is ever proven conclusively right or wrong. Years pass, people fall in and out of life, they succumb to their demons. Only devastating, lonely obsession remains.

#6620. Ina Garten’s Dancing With The Stars Confession Has Me Mourning What Could’ve Been

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

#6616. Chipotle’s Thanksgiving Eve BOGO Returns For One Night Only—Here's How To Get It

Your Wednesday night plans could use a little extra guac.

Thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before. Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving Eve BOGO deal, giving you a perfectly good excuse to grab a burrito with an old friend before the turkey, stuffing, and inevitable food coma take over.

The deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m. local time at participating U.S. restaurants, with the usual buy one entrée, get one free format we all know and love.

But, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line. You’ll need to be a Chipotle Rewards member, order at the restaurant, and scan your Rewards card at checkout. The free entrée must cost the same as or less than the one you're buying, and you can claim up to five free entrées per check. Kids’ meals don't qualify, and ordering ahead through the app, online, or for delivery won't work.

The timing has changed a bit from last year, too, when it ran from 4 p.m. all the way until closing. This time, you've got a four-hour window, so make sure that one friend you have who’s perpetually late gets the memo.

“The response last year showed us how much our guests embraced the occasion,” Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, said in a statement. According to the chain, the promotion ended up being its biggest sales-driving campaign of 2025, so a return trip was probably inevitable.

And if you’re stuffed and don’t feel like leaving the couch the next day, there’s a little something for the post-Thanksgiving crowd as well. From Friday, November 27, through Monday, November 30, Chipotle is waiving its delivery fee on eligible orders placed through its app or website with code CYBER26. You’ll need to spend at least $10 in the U.S. or $12 in Canada, and delivery menu prices may be higher, with other fees still applying.

If nothing else, it’s a convenient excuse to take a break from the annual challenge of finding increasingly creative ways to eat leftover turkey.

Black Friday is the Friday after Thanksgiving, which means that it falls on November 27 this year. But Black Friday deals are no longer confined to the single day, or even the weekend. Discounts start prior to Thanksgiving, and nearly every one lasts until at least that following Monday. Mr. Porter’s Black Friday sale kicked off on Monday, and should run through the weekend at the very least.

Cyber Monday traditionally happens the Monday after Black Friday, which means that it’s on November 30 this year. If prior years are any indication, Mr. Porter will surely be continuing their sale through Cyber Monday. #6613. Why I’m Obsessed With Vintage Coats

My collection of vintage coats is key to my personal style.

A fluffy ’90s Chantal Thomass bolero, an early 2000s Y2K Pucci dream of a trench coat, and the perfect psychedelic 1960s rainbow quilted Lord & Taylor duster: these are a few of my favorite things. In my quest and explorations of personal style, a good vintage coat never fails me. And I mean that truly: few categories hold as much power in my closet. In most situations, vintage coats are instant outfit transformers: always-on expressions of personal style that totally transport, transform, and tell (and hold) stories. They are the antithesis of a black puffer jacket.

I knew I loved vintage coats when I realized just how hard it is to find similar pieces with such an astonishing level of detail and personality today. Take, for instance, my most recent find, which is an antique raspberry silk velvet mini cape replete with ruched ruffles and a huge, tubular fabric clasp. An unlabeled, underappreciated gem, there is truly little else on this planet that looks like it. Same goes for my midi-length golden sequined trench coat with a matching sequined belt from the ’70s.

If you want a coat that speaks for you but doesn’t wear you, then I suggest a vintage option. Some of my favorite vintage coats in my closet joined my hoard by happenstance. They exist in my collection as outfit-building blocks that lead the look. Styled with maxi dresses, big skirts, or a pair of patchwork pants and a T-shirt, they truly go with everything.

I would also argue that the right vintage coat is the conversation-starter wardrobe piece that’s actually wearable. If you live in a place with a cold climate, it can also exist as the entire outfit. At a time when runways and retailers alike are pulling from the originals more than ever, it’s always fun to imagine who wore some of the most eccentric precursors.

The fun of finding the right vintage coat is a big part of it: I recommend disregarding all rules and shopping purely with your eye. I let color, texture, length, and silhouette dictate my picks, with a strong predilection for anything dramatic, extraordinary, or slightly strange. I have my favorites when it comes to vintage brands (Prada, Miu Miu, Pucci, and beyond), but a big core of my vintage coat collection is totally unbranded with no labels at all; just stories. Think: a handmade patchwork leather jacket collaged together with splices of 1920s quilts, a 1960s pumpkin orange swing coat with a chunky black faux fur collar, or my favorite Matrix-like leather jacket collected in the back of a dimly lit antique mall, waiting for me with nothing more than a Made-in-Italy tag.

The aforementioned Pucci was an accidental online find. The cropped Chantal Thomass was the textural feather jacket that I didn’t know I needed, found randomly through a reverse image search quest. And the 1960s rainbow quilted number found me: I saw her across the way in a warehouse sale and knew she was meant for me when I witnessed the incredible colors and quilting come to life against a gray, modernist backdrop. Another favorite: my liquid-effect faux snakeskin floor-length jacket looks and feels like something an iconic former showgirl or debutante would have worn.

I can’t stop collecting vintage coats, but I also see no reason not to. Most of my favorites are so rare and unique, they’d be impossible to even come close to replacing.

All of these pieces have impossibly personality-packed qualities, and they aren’t trying to be anything other than what they are. I think that’s one part of what makes vintage outerwear so great. It’s totally inimitable. The right vintage coat is proof that personal style only gets better with a little history.

#6612. Ina Garten Makes A Pretty Convincing Case For Thanksgiving Over Christmas

The Barefoot Contessa knows exactly what she wants out of a holiday.

Christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just showed up with string beans.”

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

"Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

It makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

#6608. The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

The simplest Thanksgiving side deserves better.

In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so important. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

In the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a big batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

#6607. How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Wrapping Gifts

I am one of the messiest people I know, and I come by that reputation honestly. Legend has it that when my parents first met at a party at my mom’s apartment, my dad walked up to her to say that she should probably call the police; he’d passed her bedroom while in search of the bathroom and seen the window wrenched open, with belongings strewn all over the floor. He suggested that she report a robbery—but no, she was forced to admit; that was just how she lived.

I’ve inherited her struggles with neatness and attention to detail. While other mother-daughter duos brought in perfectly stenciled posters and Balthazar-quality brownies to class presentations and bake sales, our attempts were somewhat more haphazard, typically following screaming fights in the aisles of the Staples on 81st and Broadway about what qualified as “nice” graph paper.

When it comes to Christmas, my mom and I have always been aligned on caring more about gathering the people we love to drink mulled wine and watch A Diva’s Christmas Carol for the hundredth time than creating some holiday tableau fit for Instagram. Yet this holiday season finds me in a new place in my life. Since going through a major breakup last year, I’ve tackled all kinds of things that I didn’t previously know I could do, from fixing my hyperactive car battery without a man’s paid-for help to retiling my very own bathroom floor. Was it possible that I could also become the kind of person who looked forward to—or at least didn’t totally dread—my very least favorite Christmas chore, wrapping presents?

I love shopping, I love seeing someone open what I’ve bought for them, and when I was a kid, I loved carrying already-wrapped gifts down the stairs and arranging them under the tree. But there’s something about the finicky, frilly act of wrapping and taping and bow-tying that makes me revert to that chaotic middle-schooler with the slapped-together bake sale contribution; I hate it, but I also hate hating it.

So, a few weeks ago, I decided to break the cycle. I contacted It’s A Wrap, a gift-wrapping studio and floral boutique in Studio City, Los Angeles, to ask one simple question: Could a Christmas flop like me really be taught to make a gift look great?

Y Lane, who co-owns It’s A Wrap with partner Carolyn Haywood, has seen it all when it comes to outlandishly LA-coded gifting requests. (Ask her about the time she gift-wrapped a flat-screen TV for a guy’s Playboy Bunny girlfriend on Christmas Day.) But her patience as she walked me through the basics of wrapping—assembling a box; figuring out how much tape to use; creating clean, crease-free corners—was still amazing, given that I’ve had not one but two driving instructors quit on me and, for all I know, made any number of math and science tutors seek workers’ compensation.

I’m far from Y Lane’s first student; she offers gift-wrapping lessons semi-regularly at It’s A Wrap’s cozy, Santa’s-workshop-reminiscent storefront off Tujunga Avenue (that is, if Santa’s workshop were regularly passed by shirtless bros and Alo-clad beach babes sipping iced lattes from Aroma down the street). Demand predictably increases during the holiday season, which, for her, starts well before Halloween and stretches until the beginning of January.

I got the parts with the box and the paper pretty quickly, but once we got into the specifics of bow-tying, my mind went blank. I couldn’t tie a bow in my ponytail for school spirit day or French-braid the other girls’ hair at camp to save my life, so why would I be able to now?

Slowly but surely, though, my efforts came together into a sort-of bow, which Y Lane complimented and then promptly untied, instructing me to try a few more. “The nicer the box is, the easier it is to wrap,” Y Lane told me. “The most important word in wrapping is measure.”

A few weeks later, I have a stack of neatly wrapped gifts piled up under my little pink tree impressively early. And who’s to say? Maybe I’ll also become the person who saves the wrapping paper for next year.

#6602. Cameron Diaz in ‘The Holiday’ Is My Winter Style Inspiration

Have you seen Nancy Meyers’s The Holiday recently? If not, now is the best time to rewatch the 2006 classic rom-com, as it officially turns 20 next month—and will even be returning to theaters for a limited run.

If you’ve never witnessed the genius film, it stars Cameron Diaz and Kate Winslet as two single women who do a house swap over the holidays. Hollywood editor Amanda (Diaz) relocates to the English countryside, while journalist Iris (Winslet) touches down in Los Angeles. Both end up meeting men—Jude Law and Jack Black, no less—and falling in love. While the laughs always deliver, I’m invariably awestruck by something else: Amanda’s incredibly chic wardrobe, costume designed by Marlene Stewart.

As a hotshot movie-trailer editor in Hollywood, Amanda has an elegant wardrobe that reads as one word: expensive. Throughout the movie, she almost exclusively wears white, black, and cream. (The latter buttery hue is a Nancy Meyers signature.) While Amanda’s ensembles are devoid of bold colors, prints, or logos, you can just tell that all of the clothes are luxurious—they’re all done in heavy wools and cashmeres, two snuggly materials that simply scream the holidays. It’s basically The Row before The Row was a real thing.

My favorite Amanda look comes at the beginning of the film, when her driver drops her off at her new UK holiday home. She sports an incredible brown trench coat with white shearling trim, complete with a white turtleneck, black skinny-fit trousers, and sky-high stilettos (which she wears in the snow). She then proceeds to cart her three huge suitcases—presumably filled with even more fabulous clothes!—through the snowy terrain up to the house.

As the movie continues, Amanda holds on to her effortlessly chic style. For her first night in the cozy cottage home, she drinks red wine while lounging around in a chunky cream cable-knit sweater, gray sweats, and a lilac beanie, a gray scarf slung effortlessly around her shoulder. (You have to watch her drunkenly sing “Mr. Brightside.”) I’m totally influenced to channel her quietly luxurious approach to style this holiday season, when elevated cozy dressing has its time to shine.

Amanda does deliver a few splashier evening looks in the movie too, should you need inspiration for any upcoming holiday parties. When she pops over for a visit at Jude Law’s home, she arrives wearing an incredible cream coat, unbuttoning it to reveal a black top and cream pencil skirt that’s punctuated with a wide crystal-buckle belt. “I know, I’m a tad overdressed,” she quips. “You look like my Barbie,” Law’s daughter says.

Even Amanda’s approach to formalwear is decidedly sleek and pared back. Her closet basically makes the case for timeless investment pieces: You can clearly still turn heads in a simple but well-cut silhouette. So this holiday season, you’ll find me slipping into my best Nancy Meyers neutrals too. If you find me drunk singing to the Killers at home, though, that’s none of your business.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday always falls on the Monday after Thanksgiving, which means this year it will be on November 30. Most Cyber Monday sales will extend through the end of the week, but that’s not a given. Cyber Monday begins Monday, December 2nd.

#6599. Fashion and Interiors Have Never Been Closer

Tassels, tapestries, and more: Your outfit looks like your couch, and it’s fabulous.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Scalloped lace, woven details, and perfectly curated, wearable tapestries: In 2026, fashion mirrors some of the best interior design and vice versa. All focus is on the textiles. At Isabel Marant, macramé knits and lace swinging with fringe dominated the ultra bohemian spring/summer 2027 lineup. Creative director Kim Bekker was inspired by photographer Sam Haskins’s images of women taken in the 1960s. Likewise, at The Row, a model wore a charcoal-hued blouse embellished with what looked like an elegant, supersized doily. Scarf-like tops that were tied around bodies could as easily have been vintage European throws or tablecloths. Saint Laurent, Tom Ford, and Rabanne’s sheer laces are equally houseware-ready. Dries Van Noten’s tassel coat was the outerwear crown jewel of the past few seasons coupled with the label’s new tapestry-centric coats for fall. This season, home is where the good clothes are.

Designers focused on craft and heirloom dressing through interior-inspired tactile touches in more subtle ways, too. Take, for instance, Khaite, which showcased flowy 1940s silhouettes with a hint of Victorian goth. Designer Catherine Holstein actually used a famous hotel interior as the starting point for the collection. “My husband and I spent a lot of time in Venice,” Holstein told ELLE following her show. “We always stayed at The Gritti Palace. I was having a martini at the Gritti and looking up at the ceiling.” That was the reference behind the highly detailed, handcrafted embroideries featuring flowers and horses. “I wanted all these special moments that you didn’t even see, but once you open up the clothing, everything is finished by hand.”

The statement jackets that blew up 2026’s fall fashion are also largely grounded in the kinds of textiles that feel literally at home. Think: brocades, jacquards, and lush fringe and faux fur trims. The Victorian-era textile designer William Morris (known for his hand-loom jacquard weaving) would probably love Conner Ives’s upcycled robe coats and silk-embroidered wonders.

All signs point to classic interior design inspiring accessories, too. Valentino and Dries Van Noten are both making grandmacore tapestry bags that rival your actual grandma’s couch, full of embroidery, beadwork, tassels, and fringe. Elsewhere, woven bags that are perfectly intertwined with beautiful placemats or aligned with rattan furniture are suddenly everywhere. And on a more literal note, the puffy scarf done by Loewe and Celine is basically a minimalist, wearable pillow with pizazz. Phoebe Philo and others have also cosigned the blanket coat as one of the biggest statements of the season, too.

Consider this trend fashion’s wearable security blanket: cozy, comforting, and cool.

#6592. People Are Calling The Day Before Thanksgiving ‘Green Wednesday’—And It’s Becoming A Huge Holiday

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting roasted.

Thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

If you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly announces they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery company Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence company BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

According to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The company’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok users sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

As Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those users, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

Americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an important reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

#6589. 30 Sparkling, Fringed, and Pleated Holiday Wedding Guest Dresses for Every Festive Fête

Weddings during the holiday season come with a built-in sense of joy. The venue is likely already decked out in garlands and candlelight, everyone is in a celebratory mood, and if the date falls on New Year’s Eve, there’s a midnight countdown baked right into the reception. Your outfit should match that energy. While standard winter guest attire often leans moody, a December through February fête (don’t forget about Valentine’s Day nuptials!) leaves plenty of room to play—think rich textures, high-shine finishes, and statement silhouettes.

As a bridal stylist, I always recommend letting the calendar dictate your palette. A Christmastime wedding begs for jewel tones and seasonal classics like cranberry red, deep emerald, and antique gold—all of which you’ll find at labels like Christopher John Rogers, Posse, and Simkhai. A New Year’s Eve ceremony, on the other hand, calls for anything that catches the light and has movement for the dance floor, from Altuzarra’s gold gown done up in cascading paillettes to Kallmeyer’s swingy fringe. Even a strict black-tie dress code can get a festive upgrade: Trade a standard black gown for a golden lamé maxi courtesy of Ulla Johnson. (Just be sure to check the couple’s wedding website for any specific color requests.)

Of course, a few standard wedding-guest rules still hold true. Steer clear of anything that reads as bridal—that includes winter white, no matter how tempting a cream silk slip might be. Skip the costume-like details, too: A ruby-red J.Crew mini feels spirited, while a tinsel-trimmed ensemble in the same shade can quickly veer kitschy. Beyond that, pay attention to the dress code, as that will dictate your hemline; minis and midis are fair game for less formal invitations, especially when paired with tights and a great heel. And don’t forget about a chic evening coat that’ll tie your outfit together.

Now that you know the basics, it’s time for the fun part. Browse our edit of the 30 best dresses for every holiday wedding on your calendar this winter.

#6586. Kit Keenan & Gigi Powers’s Mom’s Feta Artichoke Dip

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

Alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being quickly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. The brine from the canned artichoke hearts allows the feta to melt down in the oven, which in turn coats the artichoke hearts, creating a velvety dip. The best part about this recipe is that it’s completely customizable. My favorite variation includes adding honey, thyme, and an olive topper, which elevates the dip to a whole new level. Serve it with crunchy crostini or pita chips at your next dinner party, and your guests will go crazy.

#6585. Inside "The Tupac Tapes" With Radio Legend Angie Martinez

Going back to her early days on New York’s Hot 97, longtime radio host and veteran interviewer Angie Martinez has been getting rappers to drop their guard and engage in revealing, insightful conversations for over 30 years. Hot 97 was where you went to see Angie, Funkmaster Flex and the like if you had a new freestyle to get off, news to break, drama to address. But Martinez didn’t just get scoop; she facilitated dialogues that would often show some of the game’s most furtive rappers entirely at ease. Her show was a destination, her reporting was crucial, and her stature was reflected in a moniker: The Voice of New York.

In the years since, Angie has migrated to Power 105.1 while also moving into the podcast space. But there was always one piece of lore that loomed over her career: she was sitting on an unreleased interview with Tupac Shakur conducted shortly before his death in 1996. Now, 30 years later, she’s ready to pull back the curtain with a four-part podcast on Netflix where she plays the tapes for contemporary hip-hop luminaries like Joe Budden, Charlamagne and Big Boy, as well as figures more directly related to the events in question, like Outlawz member Edi I Mean or Biggie’s right-hand-man Lil Cease.

As the story goes: Pac became a fan of Angie and her work while incarcerated in New York, so much so that after his release he invited her to appear in the music video for his song “I Ain’t Mad at Cha.” Angie refused, and when Pac asked why she explained that a figure so closely associated with the New York rap scene appearing in that video as East Coast-West Coast tensions reached a boiling point could only be a bad look. Pac then invited her to his home to air it all out. So the Voice of New York spent over two hours with Pac hoping to come back with an interview that defused any negative energy. What she got instead was a Pac at his most turnt, angry, hurt, and vengeful, with the rapper saying things about Big, Puffy, and other New York rappers that would’ve only escalated those tensions. So Martinez sat on them, until today.

After viewing all four episodes of the podcast, I connected with Angie to find out why this was the right moment to release the interview, how she assembled such an all-star team of contributors, what she makes of the backlash to her decision, and how the The Tupac Tapes might help our fractured media landscape today.

Yeah, yeah. It's wild, right? You'll have one of those, hopefully. You’ll have a streak.

Yeah, for sure. I wasn't expecting how nostalgic... so much came up for me in [this process] because it's like a time capsule. It's not just Pac's story, but it's my story, it's about media, it's about culturally what we were doing, what we cared about [back then], how we were thinking. Nobody was thinking about healing or fucking trauma. We weren't talking about that type of stuff back then, ever.

It's just interesting to look at these tapes through a modern lens. This little blip, this little moment in history, So anyway, that part was really interesting to do with voices of the culture and people who are actually there. It's just trippy. The best word I can say is “trippy.”

Maybe, and people say that a lot, but back then we honestly weren't thinking about that. At that point in culture, we were just starting to pay attention to SoundScan numbers, we were just starting to pay attention to artists going platinum. There was no understanding of, "I'm going to be an icon." Nobody was thinking about that. We loved this shit. We were happy to be in it. We were trying to figure it out. There was no, “If I put this out, it's going to go viral.” So that's the interesting thing to me.

Yes, it could have been a big moment, but we didn't think like that. And that's the conversation to be had now, in terms of media and what we care about and what's in the front of our brain as we're making decisions and telling stories. How does this land? What's the headline? What are the clips? What’s the spin? Back then it was just like, "I'm going to go there and have this conversation, see what's up." End sentence, end thought.

It was. And the game changed so much and people care about different things now. And I get it. That's what happens with evolution, right? I really went there just to try to get people to hear what Pac was saying to me on the phone: "I don't have a problem at all with New York. That's crazy." And I was like, "Oh, shit. Nobody's heard you say that. I could go get you to say that. It would be so great." And then I go there and, obviously, it's not what he said, and that was not his temperament on that day at that time. So it wasn't a hard decision to make because I didn't want to make this worse when I was actually trying to do the opposite. Also, nobody knew what I had. So it wasn't like a public declaration of, "I'm not going to air it." It was just me quietly deciding [not to].

Well, you heard the tapes, right? The answers are there. It's like, you can hear those tapes and you can understand what would've happened, in that climate and at that time especially, but really at any time. It was sensitive. Things were happening. I mean, nobody had died, but violence was happening, gunfire was happening. So it's not too hard to figure out after you’ve heard the tapes.

Yeah, it's hard to hear. I hate that part so much, but it's what was happening at that moment.

And I'm grateful that I was able to share it with Havoc before it came out and get some context from [Outlawz member] Edi I Mean before putting this out. #6584. Kate Middleton Gets Emotional Over Her Children’s Messages in New Documentary, Heal

Kate Middleton had a special reminder of home waiting for her while doing the U.K.’s Three Peaks Challenge. In her new documentary, Heal, the Princess of Wales is surprised with loving video messages from her three children, Prince George, Princess Charlotte, and Prince Louis.

The film captures Kate’s experience climbing the highest peaks in Wales, England, and Scotland within 24 hours. The course consists of 23 miles of walking and a total ascent of over 10,000 feet.

Her younger brother, James Middleton, joined her for part of the journey and played the videos at the second summit. Prince William had recorded the messages and sent them to James to surprise his wife.

“Oh, no. Don’t. You’re gonna make me cry. No, please don’t,” Kate told her brother before watching.

Louis was the first to appear, offering his mother some words of affection and encouragement. “I really love you, and I hope you do well going up the mountain,” he said. “Remember, I’m always in your heart with you.”

George went second, telling Kate that the family is thinking of her and that she looks “really, really strong.” He assured her that she’s “gonna do a great job.”

Charlotte also shared her love, saying she and her siblings are proud of their mother and will be cheering her on.

After watching, Kate reflected on how much her children have meant throughout her cancer journey. “They gave me the reason to get out of hospital. They’re going to give me the reason to finish this challenge,” she said.

When James added, “And get home,” Kate echoed the sentiment. Before leaving the summit, she placed a small pebble among the rocks “for the kiddies.”

Heal offers a personal look at Kate’s experience with cancer, recovery, and the importance of connection and holistic care. As ELLE previously reported, the documentary also follows her conversations with others navigating serious illness.

Heal premieres on Monday, November 30, at 8 P.M. ET on NBC. It will also air on Bravo at 11:30 P.M. ET and begin streaming on Peacock on Tuesday, December 1. All funds received through the documentary’s distribution will go to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

#6582. This $20 Gadget Is My Grandpa’s Secret To Making Big-Batch Potatoes For The Holidays

It looks a little ridiculous, but I can’t stop watching it work.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

If you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

Mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up new recipes.

Since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6577. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6574. Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

While the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

Make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

When the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

#6573. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.
