#6570. The Best Nontoxic Utensils To Replace Black Plastic Spatulas (2026)

If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

More difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

New in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

Food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

There are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes

What we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

The brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes

What we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

What we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No

What we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

If steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

The same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

With five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That said, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

High-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

Not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

#6569. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6566. Welcome to Wonder by Josh Aronson

Vizcaya is a fantasy, even by Miami standards. I found myself wondering who belongs to it. Here was a forest in the middle of Miami, and beyond it, a house that seemed to have arrived from another time and place. I've always found that meeting a little magical. But I've come to understand how quickly the Florida landscape can change. The longer I spent at Vizcaya, the more I wondered how a photograph might hold some of that feeling, and what it might ask us to protect.

I grew up in South Florida. My family moved here from Toronto when I was three, and we didn't have roots here before us. I've often felt both at home in Miami and curious about my place within it. Vizcaya was part of the city's imagination long before I was invited to make pictures here. To contribute to its story as an artist felt almost difficult to believe.

Photographs have helped shape the way we see Vizcaya from its earliest days. In 1917, Mattie Edwards Hewitt photographed the estate for an issue of Architectural Review devoted to the house and gardens. Her images offered a vision of the world James Deering, Vizcaya's founder, and his collaborators had brought into being on the shore of Biscayne Bay. Today, people come here with cameras for quinceañeras, engagements, weddings, and family portraits. Those pictures find their way into albums and onto walls, carrying a little piece of Vizcaya into homes across Miami.

For Welcome to Wonder, I made a new body of photographs featuring people, animals, and landscapes across Florida. At Vizcaya, the images appear in circular frames around trees and on large banners suspended overhead, along paths that are free to walk seven days a week.

While preparing for Welcome to Wonder, I spent time looking through the estate's archive. In many of the images, people of color appeared working on or caring for the property. I began thinking about what other photographs could exist alongside them: images of young people from Miami's many communities at rest, in play, at ease in the landscape. Who gets to be seen enjoying a place like this? Who gets to imagine that it belongs to them, too?

These questions have been with me throughout my practice, from Tropicana to Florida Boys. I've traveled the state with groups of young men, making photographs in springs, swamps, forests, and along backroads. Many of us grew up in Miami and were encountering these places together for the first time. I would arrive with an idea for a scene, but the pictures were shaped by the people who came along and what the landscape offered us. I've returned to places I'd scouted and found a body of water had dried up or a shoreline had shifted. Those changes stay with me. The places that feel so expansive and enduring can be fragile, too.

I think often about Naomi Fisher's Cibachromes and Hernan Bas' paintings, the tension and theatricality their subjects seemed to find together in the landscape. Those photographs and paintings helped me imagine what it might mean to create a new world with other people, and make an image of it. With Florida Boys, I wanted to picture young men who could be tender with one another, who could rest, who could be curious. Making the photographs gave us a reason to go out and experience something together. What began as an imagined scene became part of our lives.

At Vizcaya, that world began to grow. I found myself wondering what might have happened if, after Deering died, a band of young people had moved into the estate. Who would they have loved? What would their days have looked like? What would they have discovered in the trees and along the water? I began to see the photographs as a kind of fictional archive, evidence of encounters that might have taken place here. Some pictures were made at Vizcaya; others were made elsewhere in South Florida. Together, they allowed me to imagine a landscape without the boundaries of a single property or moment in time.

For this project, I also photographed young mothers, young fathers, and young families. I thought about the lives a photograph can have after it is made. A child might one day look at an image and see their parent as a young person. A mother might see something of her own family in the gesture of someone she has never met. The photograph becomes a kind of mirror, reflecting something different depending on who we are and where we stand in our lives. I hope these pictures hold a little of that possibility for the people in them, the way they do for me.

I thought, too, about Deering. He never married, and questions about his sexuality have followed him long after his death. The historical record doesn't give us a conclusive answer. As an artist, I'm interested in the space between what a life contains and what the archive preserves. We do know that Paul Chalfin, Vizcaya's artistic director, lived here with his partner, Louis Koons. I wonder about the other private worlds that might have existed here, leaving traces we may never find.

On the Hammock Paths, photographs printed on acrylic are held in circular frames that appear to float around the trees. Along the Metrorail route, larger images hang in the canopy, printed on mesh that lets the light filter through. I was thinking about the symmetry of Vizcaya's gardens, but also about the way a circle has no beginning and no end. You can walk around a ring and find a photograph on either side. You can enter the path from the city or come upon it as you leave the museum. The images can be discovered, passed by, returned to, seen differently on any day.

Both the Hammock Paths and the Metrorail site are free and open to the public seven days a week. You don't need a ticket to spend time with the work. In a city where so much can feel out of reach, that matters. I think about the people who walk these paths every day, on their way home or with a dog, and the people who might encounter the photographs without knowing anything about Florida Boys or my collaborators. The possibility that an image could become part of someone's daily life feels like a gift and a responsibility.

Across the city, at MOCA, my commission A Sudden Leap rises from the plaza's reflecting pool. Four photographs of Florida's natural world have become sails, suspended above the water. Some of these quieter images grew out of the same journeys that gave me Florida Boys. There are no people in the pictures, but there are people moving around them, bringing their own histories and experiences to the work. I think about the sails and the journeys that have brought so many of us to Miami, including my own family. I hope the photographs might make someone want to see these places and care about what happens to them.

To have work at Vizcaya and at MOCA, my neighborhood museum, at the same time is something I'm still trying to take in. Both have given me a way to look at the place that raised me, and to offer those images back to the people who live here. The photographs at Vizcaya will eventually come down, and people will continue to walk these paths. I hope someone remembers an image the next time they pass a tree, or carries a little of the feeling of this place back into the city with them. What we choose to see, I've come to believe, has something to do with what we choose to hold dear.

Josh Aronson's Welcome to Wonder is on view at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, Miami through May 24, 2027. A Sudden Leap, Aronson's MOCA Art on the Plaza public artwork commission, is on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami through January 17, 2027.

Josh Aronson (b. 1994, Canada) is a Miami-based artist whose work explores masculinity and landscape in the American South. His photographs have appeared in The New York Times, The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Frieze, and Apartamento, among others. His first solo museum exhibition, Welcome to Wonder, is on view at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, Miami, and his first museum-commissioned public artwork, A Sudden Leap, is on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami. www.josharonson.us

#6565. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6564. Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

While this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

But getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an important role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

I got switched on to its awesomeness from a barber friend of mine—JoAnn Noriega, who cuts at Headprint Studio in San Francisco. Since this is my pick for the best pro device, I’ll leave it to her professional opinion as to why: “This device has exceptional cutting performance, providing precise and effortless trims,” she says. “I can tackle any hair type or style, plus its long-lasting battery is a game changer in my busy day.” I’m not the only one who likes that trophy-esque plating, either: “Its sleek gold finish adds a touch of luxury to my toolkit, providing me both quality and style,” Noriega says. “All of my clients comment on how they want to get cut with my gold clippers.” Adam Hurly

As much as we love the best Wahl hair trimmers, they don’t have much cool factor. On the other hand, the Bevel Pro clippers definitely pass the vibes test. (They nabbed a GQ Grooming Award in 2022.) These famous clippers have a sculptural, geometric body, an LED smart display, a sharp zero-gap blade, and an extra-powerful motor that’s strong enough for the barbershop. I’d even go so far as to call these clippers sexy. While they’re made specifically for textured hair, the zero-gap blade is also suitable for bald, coily, and short-haired guys. You can use it to trim your beard, too. Yes, it’s pricey, but there’s nothing else like it in the grooming world.

Normally, when you want to adjust a zero-gap clipper, you have to pop off the blade and manually adjust it with a tiny dial. Not so here—when you press one of the two buttons on the Bevel Pro, a second internal motor automatically opens/closes the graphite-coated stainless steel blade in 0.1mm increments. It’s so subtle you’ll have to look closely to see the difference, but every millimeter matters if you want clean lines and fades. With the included comb guards, you can trim hair from 0.0mm to 10mm. Not only are the guards sturdier than most, but they also pop on magnetically with a satisfying click. The Pro even comes with an extra-slim clipper blades for touchups. Adam Hurly

The All-in-One 9000 makes sense if you trim your beard more often than your hair and want one kit to handle both. The current bundle includes a wide clipper head, fading combs, and a separate body-shaving head, so it covers more of your routine than a conventional hair clipper. Compared with the cheaper 7000, you also get an extra hour of rated battery life and a travel case instead of a pouch. For a full buzz cut every week, though, I’d still choose a dedicated clipper.

Its wide hair head is the attachment to use for tidying the sides, with fading combs for blending between lengths. You then swap heads for the smaller jobs around your beard and body. That versatility is the attraction, but it also means keeping track of loose combs and cutters. If most of those attachments will stay in the case, the simpler Wahl Color Pro is the more sensible home-haircut purchase.

Long-term testing notes: I found the earlier Multigroom powerful enough to cut through thick patches of head hair. It became one of the few beard-and-hair multitaskers he recommended, especially for someone who trims their beard regularly and only tidies their hair occasionally. That’s the role it earns here – a useful extra job for a grooming kit, rather than the first choice for frequent full haircuts. Adam Hurly

You’ll notice this guide to the best hair trimmers for men is dominated by a single brand: Wahl. Hair trimming is very much Wahl’s turf, and they make the best hair clippers for barbers and home touch-ups alike. And according to Wahl, this is the best-selling professional hair clipper in the world (and we believe them). The Magic Clip is part of Wahl’s 5 Star professional line of products for barbers, and I love the retro-tech vibes. I also love the powerful pro-level motor, which provides even trimming so you don’t have to do multiple passes on every patch of hair.

The ubiquitous Wahl Color Pro trimmer I praised earlier is a smart choice for your first clipper (it was mine). But when you’re ready for something a bit more powerful, skip right past Wahl’s $50-$100 trimmers and pick up this tool instead. I’ve tried most of Wahl’s clippers made for home use, but the Color Pro is the only one I can really recommend. Sure, the Magic Clip is moderately pricey, but with an under-$200 price tag, it’s more affordable than other pro options from brands like Bevel. The Magic Clip comes with sturdy titanium-coated high-carbon steel blades, plus all the standard comb guards you’d find at your local barbershop. Adam Hurly

The Shortcut Pro is built for scything through hair quickly. Its palm-sized body and wide, curved blade make it easier to work around your scalp, while nine guards give you some choice over the length you leave.

That broad blade is better suited to an all-over cut than detailed fade work. When growth has gotten too long for your head shaver, it can trim it back to short stubble before you switch tools for the smooth finish. Its compact grip also leaves less handle to wrestle with behind your head. Choose it for that quick all-over reduction, rather than expecting the same precision around a fade as a narrower professional clipper.

Long-term testing notes: After five days of working from home, I usually find I’ve left it too long to go straight in with a head shaver. So I whip out my Remington QuickCut Pro – the UK equivalent of the Shortcut Pro – fling off the guard, and clip everything back to stubble. Then I finish with the shaver. I also like being able to hold the clipper in my palm when I’m reaching around the back of my head – it’s a practical shape for a job you can’t easily see. Esat Dedezade

Back in 2021, GQ called this versatile device a God-tier groomer, and it’s only gotten better since then. The MultiShape comes with a cordless handle and swappable wet/dry heads and accessories, and you can use it as a beard trimmer, electric shaver, body groomer, hair clipper, electric toothbrush, nose hair trimmer, and facial brush. You can buy some limited sets at Amazon, but I recommend going to Panasonic and customizing your MultiShape to get all the attachments you need.

The motor isn’t as powerful as professional trimmers from Wahl, BaByBlissPRO, or Bevel, but nothing comes close to matching the versatility. (There’s a reason it’s landed in our guides to the best beard trimmers, electric razors, and now hair clippers.) Plus, while most trimmers max out at 0.8” to 1” cutting lengths, the MultiShape goes all the way up to about 1.2”, making it the best hair clipper for long hair. Still, I think short-haired guys will love it, too.

This multitasking device can mow down everything to a stubble (if you so please), and then allows you to swap on that wide-set foil shaver, to take things down to a smooth finish. One device for buzz cuts, long hair, and bald guys—perfection. Adam Hurly

This is technically a trimmer, not a clipper, but it belongs on this roundup because of its superb ability to draw clean lines everywhere. It’s a barber favorite for those line ups, neckline cleanups, and its natural ability to trim at zero-gap length with minimal skin risk compared to other zero-gapping devices. If you regularly line yourself up at home, or if you want to draw clean cheek lines, necklines, sideburns, and beyond—then absolutely invest in the Andis’ Slimline Pro. Adam Hurly

It's hard to talk about clippers without mentioning Oster. (Yes, they make more than blenders—though those are good, too.) This powerful, adjustable clipper works wet or dry, has a whisper-quiet motor, and comes with guards, blending guide combs, blade oil, and a cleaning brush.

If you’re looking for a true zero-gap trimmer with the most powerful-possible motor, then this is the device you want. It’s so powerful my partner complained about the racket it made, and the 8,000rpm motor slices through even the thickest hair. Wahl calls this the first “adjustable balding blade,” and it was made for barbers working on bald cuts and fades.

The 7000 is the less expensive route to a kit that can tidy your beard, body, and hair. Its bundle includes a wide clipper head and fading combs, making it useful for occasional touch-ups between haircuts. You miss out on the 9000’s separate body-shaving head and travel case, but those extras won’t matter to everyone.

While I’m the proud owner of a regular corded Wahl Peanut, but I need to also call out the cordless option, the Peanut Li. Normally, a product loses motor power when it goes cordless, but the new version actually has a stronger 7,000rpm motor. Either of these devices are perfect for traveling, given how petite the Peanut is (just 4 inches!).

What you need from men’s hair clippers at home is much different from what barbers need in professional hair clippers. So I think the best place to start is to differentiate between the qualities that are important for the DIY hair cutter, as opposed to the barber clippers. For that advice, I got an assist from barber and STMNT Grooming Goods ambassador Jovan Figueroa. Here is his very excellent two cents on the most important qualities in a DIY hair cutter.

And then there are a few less important qualities for at-home hair clippers. These factors aren’t as important for your at-home search, though they're still good things to consider.

We look for a clipper that cuts evenly, feels steady in the hand, and makes it easy to take off the same amount of hair each time. For a home buzz cut, a set of guards that stay put and are easy to tell apart can matter more than the extra adjustments you’d find on a barber’s clipper. For fades and lineups, blade control and visibility matter more.

Adam Hurly’s years of testing clippers at home and speaking with barbers underpin this guide. Timothy Beck Werth adds his own hands-on clipper testing, along with his wider experience covering grooming gear and consumer technology. For this update, Esat Dedezade has also drawn on his grooming tests for British GQ, as credited in the entries. Advice from working barbers helps us distinguish the adjustments worth having for a fade, from the features that make a home buzz cut easier.

What is the best hair clipper for men, according to GQ?

The best men’s hair clipper for most people is Wahl’s Color Pro Cordless for its intuitive use and low cost. As we say at GQ, most people shouldn’t be giving themselves a fancy haircut. So if you require more than a simple buzz, visit the pros.

Beard trimmer vs. hair clippers: What’s the difference?

While many devices can be used as both beard trimmers and hair clippers, these devices differ in their approach to hair cutting: Beard trimmers typically require less power (since facial hair tends to be less dense) but also more precision on the average device. Meanwhile, hair clippers require more muscle to mow through thicker patches of hair, and the pros will use additional detailing devices for any fancy edgework. Also, beard trimmers are often waterproof, while hair clippers are less likely to be so.

What does zero gap mean with hair clippers?

Think of zero gapping as the ability to get an actual skin-tight clip from your hair clippers. This is done by a slight realignment of the blades so that the hairs can reach right up to those teeth. It’s usually only found on professional clippers and should be left to the pros, given the risks of cutting your skin so close to the blade. (We repeat: Proceed with caution.)

It’s best to let a professional barber or stylist fade your hair, however the general logic behind fading is to steadily decrease the clipper length (starting with a low trim or bare shave at the perimeter). If you insist on doing this yourself, then read GQ’s guide to fading your own hair.

Yes, your hair clippers are allowed on the airplane, but only in your carry-on hand baggage. Nothing with fixed batteries can be checked in the cargo.

Jovan Figueroa is a barber and hair stylist and serves as a brand ambassador for STMNT Grooming Goods.

JoAnn Noriega is a San Francisco-based barber at Headprint Studio.

#6561. Santiago Lastra Wants You to Stop Overthinking Mexican Food

Santiago Lastra might have become a mathematician if it weren’t for a box of Ritz crackers. Growing up in Cuernavaca, Mexico, the future chef behind London restaurants KOL and Fonda was the sort of kid with more of an appetite for national math competitions. “There would be four questions and five hours to answer those four questions,” he remembers. “I loved that. I wanted to do that for the rest of my life.”

Then, at 15, Lastra spotted a crab dip recipe on the back of a cracker box. He made it for his family and watched as an ordinary day changed shape around something he had cooked. “I became obsessed with the idea that you can create a special occasion just by cooking something for someone,” he says. The mathematical brain moved into the kitchen. In his first cookbook, Mexican Soul: A New Style of Cooking, Lastra writes about the magic of both disciplines: starting with a few ingredients (or figures) and a recipe (or equation) and creating something greater than the sum of its parts.

The chef has spent the past month touring the U.S. in support of the book: He’s made tacos at New York’s Santo Taco, cooked at Yucatan-style seafood spot Holbox in Los Angeles, and enlisted The Bear’s Will Poulter to put a Mexican spin on the Italian beef sandwich at Chicago’s storied Mr. Beef (the real-life inspiration for the show’s original restaurant). Along the way, he’s helped introduce American audiences to a philosophy of Mexican cooking that is as resourceful and intuitive as it is traditional and communal.

It’s an instinct that has taken Lastra on a circuitous journey back home. He started out cooking Italian food, then left Mexico for kitchens in Spain. Various fascinations with French techniques, the experimentalism of Mugaritz, and New Nordic cuisine followed. “As a young kid, when you leave Mexico, you feel that you made it,” he says. “It took me a long time to realize that what we had in Mexico was really the answer.” Lastra began applying Mexican techniques to local ingredients in Scandinavia, then traveled and cooked across 27 countries. Returning to Mexico to work on Noma’s Tulum pop-up allowed him to look at his homeland with newly curious eyes. “Being Mexican became my superpower,” he says. “I was able to share culture through food, and it opened the doors to the world for me.”

KOL was his attempt to make that realization tangible: the Marylebone restaurant that Lastra opened in 2020 cooks Mexican food through seasonal British ingredients. Fonda, its more casual and rambunctious sibling, followed four years later. “I wanted KOL to be one of the best restaurants in the world,” he says, to prove “that Mexican food should be recognized at the level of all the best cuisines in the world.” Not everyone Lastra hoped to touch could ever make it to his London spots or the global pop-ups. “What really makes a difference culturally is the food that people do at home,” he says. “Home cooking is more personal.”

Mexican Soul posed some questions. How do you cook food that feels fundamentally Mexican without fresh masa, the right dried chillies, or a specialist grocer? Lastra didn’t want readers buying a two-pound bag of chipotle for one dinner. “I had to change the way I think,” he says. He began writing new rules for the weeknight home cook, rather than an ingredients-led chef. The transition required its own education. He pored over British supermarket aisles, and during a family beach vacation, Lastra locked himself inside to watch hours of Jamie Oliver. He and his brother Eduardo, his collaborator on the book and at KOL, went into a supermarket and decreed that nothing for the shoot could be ordered elsewhere.

“It tasted great,” he recalls. “I was like, wow… I think I’ve been overcomplicating myself all my life.” Just like in his childhood math competitions, limitations could provide the route to a more interesting solution. The book’s first half teaches some culinary grammar: Sourness, heat, sweetness, smoke, fat, and masa are defined and built into pillar dishes such as guacamole and quesadillas to demonstrate how those sensations work together. “Every time I create a dish, I always see flavors,” Lastra explains. “They’re like your paintings, your colors.”

The second half gets freer: tomato and cherry aguachile, potato rajas tamales, asparagus pipián. Innovating beyond traditional Mexican cooking, this style is rooted in the cuisine’s history and designed to work with seasonal, local, and accessible ingredients from wherever its cook lives. Lastra resists the idea of Mexican food as something stuck in amber. “The most beautiful thing about Mexican cooking, or Mexican food and Mexican culture in general, is that it keeps evolving,” he says. His proudest—and most last-minute addition—was a tortilla. Nearly defeated by the challenge of creating one without corn masa, Lastra had the novel idea of using mashed potato. Combining it with potato starch, he pressed and cooked the dough, and after days of tweaking, “suddenly it worked and it puffed!” It made it into the book just before printing.

Home-testing in the Lastra household has been even sweeter. After we speak, Lastra’s mother—who almost never cooks—is making the book’s mackerel a la Veracruzana for her sons. She’s already sending photographs as she shops for ingredients. “I think she’s never cooked a specific recipe from a cookbook in her life,” he says. “So that’s going to be such a highlight.”

Below, Santiago Lastra’s recipe for albóndigas and Mexican rice, two ways.

Meatballs came to Mexico from the Middle East during the colonial period. They’re a classic of central Mexican home cooking, and are also served in casual eateries called fondas, where they are served with rice and bread or tortillas. The sauces they are served with vary from loose sauces made with cooked green tomatillos to rich tomato and guajillo chilli-based broths. I serve mine in a tomato caldillo with Mexican rice—a classic from our hometown. This is one of my favorite Mexican dishes, and one I would often choose to make if I am hosting friends for dinner.

Red rice is present at most lunches for any Mexican growing up, whether at home or eaten in a fonda. The preparation is simple: rice with peas and carrots, cooked in a tomato and chilli caldillo. The result is a spicy, umami rice with a beautiful color. Serve with stews and tortillas.

Like the red version, this preparation adds a bit of spice, texture, and umami to plain rice. It’s served with all sorts of stews and other dishes in central Mexico, and also with broths like chicken consomé—the kind your mom might make for you when you’re unwell. Fresh jalapeños add a beautiful spicy finish. Perfect with chicken or any other proteins and refried beans.

#6560. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6559. Sheet-Pan Chicken Caesar Salad

This is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

Whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

#6556. The Best Cold-Weather Cocktails to Drink This Holiday Season

I typically take a less-is-more approach when it comes to my beverage choices. Having been burned one too many times by the flavor-packed ‘ingenuity’ of a bar’s signature cocktail, I’ve come to the conclusion that a martini, Negroni, or gin and tonic are better suited to my spartan palate. But once the holidays roll around, well, my fidelity to simplicity goes out the window, and I am an enthusiastic proprietor of the cozy cocktail.

What’s a cozy cocktail? Exactly what you think it is. A spirited sip that summons the mood of a crackling fireplace and the flavors of a Christmas kitchen. That transports you to a snowed-in cabin in Lapland, or a bustling holiday market in Germany. And I’m not talking about kitschy cocktails afflicted by crushed-up candy canes and artificial syrups—no, no. These are recipes that chase the outer limits of mixology, bringing together all that is merry and bright and elegantly transmuting it into your glass.

There are many paths a cold-weather cocktail may take. Traditional classics, like eggnog and hot toddies, are always welcome. For something theatrical, a smoked tipple does the trick (top marks for those performed tableside). For an off-the-charts cozy cocktail, those infused with seasonal spices will leave you deliriously jolly. And if you can’t bear to part ways with your old fashioned or espresso martini, take solace in knowing there are ways to ‘winter-fy’ these quintessential favorites.

If you’re ready to raise a glass of something cozy in the coming weeks, let the guide below inform your order. And for those who wish to whip up cocktails for a festive fête at home, don’t miss the recipes at the end. Bar carts at the ready!

The holidays present a decadent array of creamy cocktails calibrated specifically for the season. Take eggnog, for example. This rich tipple originated from a hot, milky, ale-adjacent drink called ‘posset’ that was enjoyed during Britain’s medieval era. Somewhere along the timeline, eggs joined the party, and several hundred years later, we’ve arrived at our modern-day recipes that consist of milk, heavy whipping cream, sugar, eggs, and nutmeg (spiked with rum, bourbon, or brandy). A boozy holiday milkshake, if you like.

Over at Smithereens in the East Village, head bartender Jacob Dorman wanted to make an eggnog with their in-house label rum, but decided to do an egg flip variation to show the versatility of the rum. (For reference, the main difference between an egg flip and eggnog is that a traditional flip leaves the dairy out.) “People always think of rum as a tropical spirit, but it can be warming and comforting too,” Dorman says. He uses a squash amaro for his flip, which “is like drinking pumpkin pie (in a good way).”

Another creamy drink that foregoes the use of eggs is coquito. This Puerto Rican holiday cocktail typically uses coconut milk, cream of coconut, evaporated milk, sweetened condensed milk, vanilla extract, cinnamon, and ground nutmeg—spiked with rum. In a similar spirit, at The Wig Shop in Boston, beverage director Oscar Simoza is currently serving up a Venezuelan-inspired take on eggnog. It’s made with banana peel-infused rum, batido de cambur (ripe banana and milk), and arequipe (caramelized milk). Notes of anise and cinnamon, alongside a hint of amaro, come together for a cocktail that is sublimely silky.

The Brandy Alexander is another perennial classic. It’s made with brandy or cognac, dark crème de cacao, heavy cream, and freshly grated nutmeg for garnish. One of my favorite variations is at Bar Rêve in Cobble Hill. “Ours is an après-ski homage,” co-founder Victor Triebel says. They pair a base of cognac with a layer of Frangelico whipped cream, finished with freshly grated nutmeg. “There’s nothing more luxurious than a warming brandy cocktail to end the evening,” Triebel adds.

During the chilliest months of the year, a cocktail encircled by fragrant smoke is just what the doctor ordered. Last winter, I found myself in the grand lobby of the Carlton Hotel St. Moritz, where drinks are served beside a stone fireplace and arrive via trolley cart. Their Piz Nair Mule—presented in a glass case—is inspired by a mountain that rises 3,057 meters above the Engadin Valley. Once the case is opened, a gentle cloud of smoke escapes, revealing the cocktail and miniature alpine landscape, complete with a moss-covered mountain and tiny mountaineers traversing the summit. The cocktail itself is a soothing blend of fresh thyme and rosemary, spicy ginger, and lime.

If you can’t make it all the way to Switzerland this year, fret not, because San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, California, has an entire menu dedicated to its tableside smoked cocktails. I’ve had the Smoking Pig Poke, which combines rye whiskey, averna, Luxardo maraschino, and a bacon-wrapped brandied cherry—all smoked with cherry wood. (They also serve cocktails smoked with oak, hickory, pecan, and pear woods—in case you’re picky about such things.) And if you’d like to impress your friends and try your hand at your own smoked cocktails, this smoke infuser would make an excellent holiday gift.

Distilling the holiday season’s rich baking spices into a cocktail is nothing short of alchemy. Cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, cardamom, allspice—each offers its own shade of warmth, and can be used as liquor infusions, spiced syrups, bitters, or simply garnishes.

At the newly opened Thai restaurant, Hommali, head bartender Patrick Cura created their Horchata Oolong cocktail, blending tequila, shochu, and sweet vermouth that’s been infused with oolong and umami bitters. “We torch a cinnamon stick over the glass for the garnish so you get an initial hit of baking spice at the first sip,” he shares. “It feels like a warm hug in a glass, which is particularly enjoyable when the temps start to drop.”

Over at The Portrait Bar inside The Fifth Avenue Hotel, bar director Darryl Chan’s Marrakesh cocktail is inspired by the spice markets of Morocco. And further downtown at abcV in the Flatiron District, the Saffron Mylk rum cocktail is a blend of spices and saffron, heated with oat milk and honey, then finished with lashings of nutmeg. “The aroma from the nutmeg gives a wonderful warmth, with the heady spice evoking the holidays,” Chris Moore, director of beverage at Jean-Georges Restaurants, says.

And if you’re searching for something a bit lighter, head for Williamsburg dive Shenanigans for their spiced vodka cran, featuring vodka, mulled wine with baking spices, lemon, and soda. (Starting December 2, Shenanigans will kick off their holiday pop-up serving festive cocktails through the new year—make haste.)

While the holidays have spurred legendary cocktail creations aplenty, if you prefer to stick to what you know, look for seasonal riffs on the classics. Hot cocoa is a wonderful place to start. You can spike your beloved hot chocolate with everything from aged rum and bourbon to cointreau and Bailey’s Irish cream. At Limo Bar in the East Village, their Santa’s Coffee cocktail dials up the cozy by pairing Irish whiskey and coffee with maple syrup and salted maple cream.

On a recent visit to the newly opened Bar CC, I ordered the Vesuvio, which is their spin on a coffee Boulevardier. The cocktail layers coffee-infused bourbon with cacao, tonic bean, amontillado sherry, Barolo Chinato, Campari, and Cappelletti rosso. The cocktail is then clarified with heated milk that’s been enriched with mascarpone. (Professional mixology here; do not attempt at home.) But wait! I haven’t even arrived at the best part: an edible lace doily is delicately draped over the glass, resulting in the most elegant riff on a Boulevardier you or I have ever encountered.

For the espresso martini devout among us, head for Pinky Swear to order the Cloud 9, which is an espresso martini garnished with a torched marshmallow. Or if you’re an old fashioned fanatic, take note of the Outtake at New Orleans’s Cure bar, which is seasoned with warm walnut and crisp ginger. Even clear spirits can receive the holiday treatment—at Dandelion in the West Village, their Poire None cocktail swirls together tequila, mezcal, ginger, allspice, yellow Chartreuse, and pear cider for an autumnal riff on the timeless mule. And at Dean’s, rather than relying on brandy or whiskey to conjure the cozies, their winter-friendly take on a classic sbagliato features sloe gin and elderflower liqueur for a deeper, fruitier character.

When in doubt, if you have a go-to cocktail but want to get into the spirit of the season, ask your bartender what they’ve got up their sleeve.

Not drinking alcohol? There are plenty of cozy mocktails that still fit the prompt. Beverages like eggnog, coquito, hot toddies, and hot chocolate can all be created with as much depth and complexity as their boozy counterparts—just skip the liquor part at the end. The Pear of Aces at Golden Steer is an aromatic hot toddy that simmers whole cloves, cinnamon, and star anise with lush pear nectar and melted lemon sherbet.

Or there’s the spirit-free amaretto sour at The Lobby Bar inside Hotel Chelsea, which doubles down on roasted flavors. This cocktail uses a zero-proof Amaretto liqueur made of roasted almonds from Puglia, plus a roasted green tea that’s acidified with lemon juice. “The cocktail is served up with a floater of honey-miso whipped cream, to replicate the head of egg white foam from a traditional sour-style cocktail,” shares Brian Evans, the director of bars at Sunday Hospitality.

Throwing a holiday party and need a few cozy cocktail ideas? Continue below for libations that will get everyone into the spirit of the season.

Directions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a coupe and garnish with grated chocolate.

“The Grasshopper is usually credited to Tujague's in New Orleans. It's a simple drink: crème de menthe, crème de cacao, and a splash of Franca menta and fresh cream, shaken until frothy and served a cool, pale green. Mint and chocolate taste like candy canes and peppermint bark, and the cream makes it smooth and soft. The green looks right at home by a tree or under twinkling lights. It's light and festive, a little nostalgic, and closer to dessert in a glass than to a cocktail” - Linden Pride, principal, Dante Elizabeth Street

Directions: Run the apples through an extractor to separate the juice from the solids, letting the juice pour directly into a frothing pitcher. Add the sauce and bourbon. Steam all ingredients with a steam wand as though preparing milk for a latte. Pour into a heated mug.

Toddy Sauce Directions: Toast eight cinnamon sticks and four grams of whole black pepper in a pot. Add 650 grams Lambic (Duchess de Bourgogne), 650 grams Maple syrup, 12 grams turmeric and nine grams black pepper. Bring to a quick boil then lower to a simmer for 10 minutes. Cool and strain into a deli.

“Fresh pressed green apples are some of my favorite things to work with because the texture is so frothy coming out of the Breville. Steaming them doubles down on the intensity of the technique. The spice blend of turmeric, black pepper, and cinnamon evokes strong winter memories without falling into ‘pumpkin spice’ or Angostura bitters. Everything remains both familiar and impossibly new.” - Owen Gibler, Beverage Director, Bar Roza

Directions: Beat egg yolks and sugars until lightened in color and texture. In a separate bowl, combine dairy, spirits, salt, and nutmeg. Slowly stream the mixture into the beaten egg yolks and sugar while mixing. Once homogeneous, transfer to a sterile glass container and refrigerate for at least one week, ideally one month. Serve with freshly grated nutmeg.

“An elevated take on the holiday classic, Beckon’s Aged Eggnog is prepared months in advance, allowing bonded bourbon, Armagnac, aged and white rum to mellow alongside egg yolks, cream, milk, sugar and nutmeg. Aged for at least one week (though a month is even better), the high-proof spirits develop an almost cheesecake-like tang, resulting in a rich, warming cocktail finished simply with freshly grated nutmeg.” - Joseph Buckley, beverage director, Paired Hospitality

#6555. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6554. Brown Butter Sage Chicken Skillet

Boasting a brief ingredient list and a short cooking time, this easy chicken dish is one you’ll be making all season. Basic butter becomes the star here—it turns brown and nutty, then gets infused with sage and garlic for a savory sauce that’s basted over simply seasoned chicken breasts. A big squeeze of lemon, plus its zest, helps balance the richness. This skillet dinner is perfect for a speedy weeknight meal, but it’s also special enough for company.

The protein:You don’t have to limit yourself to chicken here. Feel free to replace the breasts with pork chops, shrimp, scallops, or skinless salmon or halibut fillets. Simply adjust the cooking time to properly cook the protein, but be sure to maintain a medium heat. While meat and fish are often cooked on medium-high heat for a nice char, it needs to be a bit lower to avoid bitter residue in the pan, since the butter will be browned immediately afterward.

The crunch:The sage leaves crisp while the butter browns, but there are also ways to add more texture. Stirring in a handful of slivered almonds toward the end of cooking adds to the nuttiness of the dish; pine nuts, pistachios, or roughly chopped walnuts would also work. If you have a container of them, feel free to sprinkle some fried onions on top tableside.

Storage and serving ideas:This is not a make-ahead situation; it should be eaten immediately after it’s cooked. Serve with a simple salad dressed in a light vinaigrette to balance the richness. To soak up the sauce, mashed potatoes—traditional or sweet—are ideal. Or, to add another nutty element, roast some Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, or butternut squash to eat alongside and round out the meal.

#6553. 57 Food Gifts We’re Giving (and Secretly Hoping to Get) in 2026

It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting. After all, getting your shopping done now means you can focus on the important things once the holidays actually roll around—you know, like spending time with family, cooking a festive feast, and enjoying plenty of mulled cider and wine. If you’re in need of gifts for the food people in your life, look no further. These are the 57 gifts we’re planning to give (or hoping to receive) this year.

A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!). Tailor your pick to your giftee’s caffeine preferences to make it feel more personal: opt for an oversized mug for the friend who needs drip coffee on an IV, or a more petite cup for the cappuccino drinker.

I recently added these elegant tumblers to my collection thinking they’d be great for dinner parties, and they are—but they’ve also become my new favorite everyday water and iced latte glasses, because while they’re beautiful, they feel sturdy enough for daily use. They bring a smile to my face every time I use them, which is exactly what a great gift should do, isn’t it?

An olive oil can is the kind of thing that’s meant to live on your counter, so why not upgrade to a beautiful one? This sleek stainless-steel model from Seattle-based design studio Holcomb has been in my gifting rotation since it was released. It goes with multiple different home aesthetics and looks equally at home by the stove as it does on a dinner party table.

Give the designated host friend a set of whimsical spiral-tipped serving utensils to use at their next dinner party. And don’t worry, they’re dishwasher-safe.

Buttered toast is a perfect food, in my opinion, and anyone that agrees will adore this handblown glass butter keeper from East Fork. Its design ensures your butter can be kept at room temperature for weeks without spoiling, which means it’ll stay perfectly spreadable and ready to be swiped across whatever carbs you choose.

Any friend who cooks will appreciate receiving this set of ramekins from cult-favorite pottery brand East Fork. At four ounces, they’re a versatile size that works for equally as well for portioning mise en place as it does for serving condiments or sauces.

This stylish pepper grinder looks incredibly cool, but it’s also made with function in mind. That swanky-looking handle? It’s designed to be ergonomic, able to be held and twisted in myriad ways depending on what’s most comfortable for the user. This gift set pairs the grinder with Piper’s 50-50 blend of black and red peppercorns, portioned into four individual packets to ensure the spices stay fresh.

These stunning wood cutting boards are truly heirloom-worthy, handcrafted by expert woodworkers from sturdy hardwood. They’re versatile pieces that are durable enough to be your everyday chopping boards and beautiful enough to serve as serving vessels for cheese and charcuterie.

You can’t go wrong with a beautiful vase, especially if you fill that vase with a bouquet of fresh flowers. This colorful glass number is sure to earn your giftee compliments, and I love that it’s hand-blown, which means every piece is one-of-a-kind.

You never know when you need a large bowl until you find yourself in need of a large bowl. Any person who likes to host should have a few attractive options on hand, and a splatter enamelware bowl is a pretty timeless choice.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

Get the friend who nerds out on coffee roasting and fermentation processes a subscription to Podium Coffee Club’s Platinum tier, which sources its monthly beans from award-winning roasters across the country. The Platinum tier is focused on rare coffee varietals made using experimental techniques, so it’s perfect for someone who likes an expressive, unique roast.

This gift set brings a taste of Richard Christiansen’s Flamingo Estate to your pantry. It’s full of high-quality products you’ll actually use—no weird spice blends or waxy chocolates here.

For the friend who would gladly eat tinned fish for dinner every night, I suggest this 10-pack of greatest hits from Fishwife. It’s got a little bit of everything, from the brand’s smoked salmon collab with Fly By Jing to the fan-favorite Smoked Rainbow Trout with Chimichurri, plus limited edition Little Sardines, which are available only as a part of holiday sets.

We all know someone who finishes every dish with flaky salt. Get them this pack of tins from Jacobsen Salt Co., each of which is filled with a different kind of infused salt. They’re small enough to slip into even the tiniest of purses, so your salt-loving friend will never be without their favorite flaky finisher.

When in doubt, opt for wine. But instead of picking up a random bottle, treat your giftee to a month (or three or six!) of deliveries from New York City wine bar and shop Parcelle, whose Wine Drop subscription service has been a longtime BA fave. Choose between red, white, rare, or a curated monthly mix, and Parcelle will take care of the rest.

If you know somebody with a matcha habit that’s burning a hole through their wallet, they’d probably appreciate a set of ceremonial-grade powders from a tried-and-true brand like Matchaful. This set is also perfect for demonstrating just how different matcha powders can be.

Balsamic Vinegar of Modena & White Condiment Set

Food storage is about as practical as gifts get, but Misenware makes it feel special. Our testing samples vanished from the BA office almost instantly, and plenty of staffers bought their own once we had run out. The stainless-steel containers seal so tightly that we have no fear of soup leaking in a work bag. They’re microwave-safe, they won’t stain, and they held up when we jumped up and down on them.
