#6495. Inside the Making of Dolly Alderton’s Lavish New ‘Pride and Prejudice’

As a generation awaits its own adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, screenwriter Dolly Alderton shares her funny, intimate, and illuminating day-to-day diary of making the television event of the year.

Meeting Dame Emma Thompson for tea seems like the perfect place to start this diary. An hour with her has been more useful than every book and radio programme and essay I’ve read about Austen in the last year. She answers my long list of questions so generously and thoughtfully. A few examples of her wisdom: 90 percent of Austen is the casting; a good comedy editor will make or break it; we must ignore the temptation to over-score and let the dialogue speak for itself; I must prepare a document of additional dialogue so the language stays precise and the actors don’t “Regency ad-lib”; I have to make the stakes of marriage clear for a modern audience; I must not be scared of the Janeites. (“They have the books. Let them enjoy the books.”)

As I leave, she gives me a big hug. “Mate, it’s gonna be brilliant.” True sisterhood.

The day I have been dreading. Cuts. Lisa (producer) reassured me by saying she thinks we can make cuts that are “surgical, with a scalpel” rather than “lopping great chunks out.”

We have to lose Lydia and Mrs. Forster sea-bathing, but I’ve insisted we keep the sea-bathing machines. Devastatingly, we’re losing Mr. Collins sneaking out of Longbourn down a drainpipe—a day of shooting for one moment of slapstick. Ongoing debate about whether we can keep Lizzy and Jane finding the Netherfield flushing toilet. There aren’t any original Georgian ones around and it will cost £15k to build. Discussion of whether £15k is too expensive for a joke. I think not, but then I have regularly lost much more, dignity-wise if not financially, to secure a laugh.

The Meryton Harvest Market is edging towards the guillotine. This was already a compromise on what I originally wrote, which was a Regency autumn fair with swings, puppet shows, wrestling, toffee apples, and a fortune teller. Now it’s looking like it’s going to be one extra selling a marrow. Lisa cleverly suggested she look into our “livestock budget” to see if it might be cheaper to fill all of Meryton with a load of sheep being traded, as at least that will fill the frame and feel busy and agricultural.

All in all, today was not as bad as I thought it was going to be. Have my work cut out incorporating cuts, our director Euros’s notes, production notes, and final editorial notes into new drafts by next Friday. Lisa as I leave: “I am afraid next week is going to be a horrible week for you.”

Go see Loyle Carner at a very, very hot Hackney church. Paralytic woman drenched in sweat corners me to say she is obsessed with Pride and Prejudice and she hopes our adaptation doesn’t disappoint. No pressure.

We got Louis Partridge! We got Louis Partridge! My number-one choice for Wickham—a man who looks like he really could ruin your life. Hooray! I always forget how much casting feels like dating. When they turn you down, it makes you question everything about your show. When they say yes, it really does feel like they want to go out with you. I’m going out with Louis Partridge.

Spend the morning in London North Studios being shown racks and racks of beautiful costumes. Have already taken a shine to Mr. Bennet’s embroidered dressing gown and plot to nab it at wrap. I sit in on a Bennet family rehearsal—Rufus (Sewell) talks about the importance of the scene in the book in which Mr. Bennet recognises his own failings as a negligent father.

Lemonia for a cast dinner. Louis and I grill Rufus about hell-raising in Primrose Hill in the ’90s. I am put in between Louis and Daryl (McCormack) and Will (executive producer) later observes that I look very smug about it. Louis and I talk about Mary Oliver poetry; Daryl and I talk about Rome, where he is off to on a job after P&P. Worry I was too forceful with my restaurant recommendations, a bad habit of mine. I just can’t bear the thought of Daryl McCormack having a sub-par carbonara.

I ask them what jobs they would have done if they weren’t actors. Louis, documentarian; Daryl, wildlife photographer; Emma (Corrin), primary school teacher. Night ends with Manda (Netflix executive producer), Lisa, and I discussing the mesmerising shade of Daryl’s eyes when we realise he’s behind us in earshot, waiting for his Uber. I’m sure he’s used to it.

Emma Corrin, Olivia Colman, and Freya Mavor take on one of the more famous families in literature. Now they’re in a WhatsApp group called “The Bennet Bitches.” Corrin wears a Burberry faille jacket. Vintage skirt from the Arc London. Jil Sander neck ruffle. Cartier jewelry. Colman wears a Michael Kors Collection silk shawl and gloves. Vintage jacquard jacket and skirt from Rellik. Neous shoes. Mavor wears a Celine satin top. Vintage jacquard skirt from Rellik.

Read-through day. So useful for the writing process, because it’s the first time you hear humans saying your lines and the first time you can deduce what sounds natural and what sounds written. But also a horrible day for a writer, because the actors are new to the dialogue and only semi-performing while sitting down, so it can make everything feel a little flat. A friend of mine, who is a TV showrunner, says she hates read-throughs because it feels like everyone is reading from her diary “in a mocking voice.”

Do a little speech to kick things off and try not to be too mawkish, despite feeling overwhelmed with excitement and gratitude. I say it’s like looking at my fantasy football team, but I was allowed to select players from IMDb.

Episodes one to three go well—much better than I expected. Fiona Shaw’s formidable Lady Catherine a particular standout, but all of them are brilliant. We are so lucky to have each and every one of them.

Read-through of episodes four, five, and six, all of us weeping in the last few scenes of six. Pull strange faces trying to hold back the tears as surely there is nothing more unbecoming than being visibly moved by your own script. Regency boot camp for the cast afterwards, followed by Netflix’s “respect workshop.” I can’t help but text Jamie (Demetriou) afterwards and ask what he learnt. He says the highlight was Jack (Lowden) being asked if it’s OK to date fellow actors from set. His reply: “I fuckin’ hope so ’cos I married one.”

Day one of shooting! At the Golden Parsonage in Hertfordshire, our Longbourn, where we essentially move into until December. The first scene is a very hungover Mrs. Bennet walking through the garden with the Bennet sisters the morning after the Netherfield ball. I think we should have Olivia (Colman) seem notably nauseous, but Lisa thinks that’s overcooking it. We get one slightly vommy take for me.

Everyone paranoid about paps. I think we’ve managed to dodge them—one of the reasons we chose the Golden Parsonage is that all its surrounding land is private property.

Emma’s dog is here who is like a giant Beanie Baby. I have been assured he will be on set a lot.

Sister act. As Lizzy and Jane Bennet, Corrin and Mavor are far from straightfoward ingenues. Austen would approve. Corrin wears a three-piece suit and shirt from Schiaparelli. Neous boots. Cartier gold and diamond earrings. Mavor wears a pinstripe suit from Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello. Emporio Armani cotton shirt with neck-tie. Cartier earrings.

Everyone falling more and more in love with Louis. Charlotte (head of costume) tells me he has been crocheting a little hat for his friends who are expecting a baby. And during the lunch break yesterday, he went into a nearby field to sit and play guitar.

Charlotte walks us through the costume rails—standouts include a playfully embroidered waistcoat for Lizzy, lots of icy blues for Jane, which suit Freya (Mavor)’s complexion perfectly. And a dress so beautiful for Lydia that Rhea (Norwood) has said she wants to be buried in it. I’m so glad we went for Charlotte and her eye for original textiles. So many of the fabrics date back to the 1800s.

Lisa has pointed out that we’ve got to change a line of Wickham’s. On a Ramsgate beach, he compares the colour of Georgiana’s eyes with the colour of the sea, but we’ve just cast Isabella, who has brown eyes. Lisa wonders if we keep it as is and if there’s a joke to be made about the colour of the Kent coastline.

Honey-glazed carrots for lunch today, which Euros has declared “a revelation.”

Fucking paps. They managed to get a photo of Emma and Freya’s first scene on the Longbourn roof. Apparently the photographer was hiding in a tree up to a mile away and still managed to get pictures! Most of them are of Emma and Freya chatting and on their phones between set-ups. My favourite comment under the article: “Lizzy Bennet would NOT have had a mobile phone. This is NOT historically accurate.”

At lunch, Jack and I stand in the drizzle eating cheesecake and discuss Darcy. He’s trying to get under the skin of him. I had the same thing when I first started writing Darcy—he’s a hard character to understand. Jack asks me why Elizabeth is attracted to him—I tell him that Darcy is capable; a man of action, rather than just words. Jack points out that he’s got servants that do everything for him, which is a fair point. I talk about how capability and reliability can be more than just putting up shelves, etc.

Louis is as chivalrous as ever, standing up and offering me a chair and asking me about my weekend. “Like you’re his grandma?” Will asks flatly, when I boast of this later.

Shooting London scenes in Spitalfields today. More nuisance paps and people dangling out of windows taking videos. Lisa tells me that there’s one pap, called Ralph, who is always hanging about, whingeing to her that he can’t get good photos and they don’t sell for as much as they used to. “At this point I may as well add him to the catering numbers,” she mutters.

Poor Jack having to do a lot of silent staring out of carriage windows. Darcy really is such a hard part in so many ways. So unknowable and brooding for such a hefty portion of the story. Mostly mute, deep-in-thought acting for Jack this first month of filming. When I watch the rushes, I hear him say, “I’ve got nothing going on behind my eyes, I should have never taken this job,” as he is directed to get in and out of a carriage for the 100th time.

Lowden wears an Ann Demeulemeester cotton shirt with ruffled collar and cuffs. Vintage trousers from Costume Studio. Ferragamo shoes.

Hungover. Claude (set PA) gets me a fry-up and I save her the sausages as a thank you. We’re shooting the interiors of Hunsford today in a house near Shepperton. It is boiling hot and cloudy—the worst kind of weather. Jamie’s in today. He tells me that whenever he’s asked to do background Regency conversation, he turns to the person next to him and asks, “Is your father fond of horses?”

Nancy Meyers has posted on Instagram Stories about how she’s sick of seeing pap shots from our set and she wants Pride and Prejudice to be a surprise when it comes out.

Olivia, Emma, and the Bennet sisters are all on a WhatsApp group called The Bennet Bitches.

Feel like Lizzy as we drive into our Pemberley location. My heart flutters—I am so glad that this is our Pemberley. It was always my first choice. It’s breathtaking, bucolic, epic, and so, so romantic. I arrive just in time to see the final set-ups of Lizzy and Darcy’s unexpected meeting. It is the first time we see any softness between them, and it’s the first time we see the true Darcy rather than the carapace he presents to the world. We probably had more meetings about this scene than any other scene across the whole show. It’s the moment we have to see Darcy as a man; as a human, and not just a status. We have to see the heart and soul and loins under all his finery and front.

There were so many bad versions of this part of the story that I wrote and ended up in the bin—one of the more memorable ones was “the horny tree” draft, where Darcy shows Lizzy the oldest trees on the Pemberley estate and talks in cack-handed metaphors about how you can only see the true colour of the bark when you are close to it. Everyone hated it apart from Lisa. As we approach the house, we lament the loss of horny tree and choose which tree we would have used for that scene. She would have gone for a rather girth-y chestnut near unit base.

I stand on the terrace and watch the scene on Euros’s monitor. Jack and Emma’s performances are beautiful—halting, delicate, vulnerable. I think it will work really well, particularly in the vast grandeur of the surroundings. The last direction Euros calls out before they do their final take: “Remember Emma, he is the north to your south. Action!” This is why he is the perfect director for this job. Amongst many other things, he has a heart that understands true romance.

Lisa drives us to the hotel and, pleasingly, the Hovis advert music plays on Classic FM as we approach Harrogate. Wagamama for dinner. Good, obviously, but will forever mourn kare lomen after its cruel disappearance from the menu.

Daryl is shooting today, looking dashing in his double waistcoat. I wish boys dressed like this now. Although he tells me his britches were so tight, they split when he sat down on the first day of filming.

Siena and Saffron (playing the Bingley sisters) are gloriously bitchy in their scene today. It’s an iconic passage from the book, when Caroline feels so threatened by Lizzy’s surprise visit at Pemberley, she lists all the physical characteristics she dislikes about her to try to get close to Darcy, who instead swoops to Lizzy’s defence. Siena is so good at keeping Caroline on just the right side of catty, so it is enjoyable without becoming too panto. Isabella (playing Georgiana Darcy) also shines in her performance today—sweet without being saccharine. She’s been practising her piano on a keyboard in her trailer.

Lisa tells me that Ralph the pap was waiting with a camera, armpit deep in heather, at our remote filming location earlier this week. When Lisa asked who gave him a tip-off, he claimed he wasn’t tipped off, but rather his dad—by total coincidence!—had been in the Peak District and saw some signs for filming so told Ralph in case there was something for him to photograph. Ralph followed the signs and what do you know?! It was the Pride and Prejudice production. Funny how life goes, eh.

A love for all seasons. Colman and Rufus Sewell reimagine Mrs. and Mr. Bennet with a sparkling wit and—whisper it—new levels of romance. Colman wears a McQueen tweed opera coat. Sacai trousers. Sophie Bille Brahe pearl earrings and ring. Sewell wears a Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello wool coat. Ferragamo poplin shirt and wool trousers. Vintage cravat from Costume Studio.

Turn 37. Pub, home, two birthday cakes, Antiques Roadshow. Perfect.

Our first day fully bedded into Longbourn. All of us swooning over the paint colour on the cornicing and panels (aquatic blue). Chloë (director of photography) tells me that it’s a colour that suits wood, candlelight, and skin.

The exterior of the house is still being bedecked with vegetation. The seasons and movement of a year are so important in Austen novels, but particularly in Pride and Prejudice. We’re leaning heavily on nature to help us tell that story. I desperately want to have a go on the cherry picker but Lisa forbids it for health and safety reasons.

Another baked potato for lunch. I can’t seem to opt for anything else. Baby pheasants hopping around the grounds. Get home to a belated birthday present from Aunty Susan—a picture book called A Guinea Pig Pride & Prejudice. Does what it says on the tin.

We’ve all descended on Rye to shoot Meryton scenes. Laura (executive producer) is here with her two gorgeous little girls who are extras in one of the scenes. They get to keep their bonnets.

Kitty and Lydia rushes are in and their chemistry is exactly what I had hoped it would be—so giggly and alive.

Lots of livestock for the market scenes, including baby goats, which is obviously heaven, but the baby goat handler makes it clear that she doesn’t approve of my incessant petting.

We’re shooting an absolutely enormous scene, about seven pages. I don’t know what I was thinking. So much blocking to do, so many characters coming in and out. Bree the dog, playing Charlotte Lucas (played by Jasmine Blackborow)’s dog, is here and none of us know why, she’s not in any of the Rye scenes.

Today I get to witness the utterance of the line: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” I often think of Jane Austen and what she would have made of all these interpretations and imaginings of her work. I sent Emma (Thompson) an email the night before we started shooting and she wrote a kind and thoughtful reply telling me that Jane would be by my side. “She was—well—a seer, a weird sister, a person who did what she could within the boundaries.”

Head to my favourite place, the costume truck, for a hang. They spray all the costumes with a mixture of vodka and eucalyptus to freshen them up because some of the fabrics are so delicate and old they can’t take detergent. Charlotte shows us a sketch for a fabulous Lady Catherine costume. All black with a high neck—she will look like an elegant crow.

Rufus believes actors should actually eat in eating scenes so this morning he had to get through countless sausages and a mound of buttered toast for multiple takes of a breakfast scene.

Dinner with my friend Lara who is interviewing Bonnie Blue tomorrow. She wants to find a new line of questioning. Apparently Bonnie is a jigsaw enthusiast, which has been overlooked thus far for obvious reasons.

Huge confrontation scene between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet today. Olivia likes shouting in scenes because she’s not a shouter in real life.

Head out for the evening, hop onto the Victoria line only to bump into Fiona on the same carriage. She introduces me to her lovely wife, who is an economist. We talk about the importance of having a partner who is not in the same industry as you. Forever grateful that I didn’t end up with an actor or a writer. They are on their way to the Young Vic, I am on my way to Elizabeth Day’s book launch. I can’t find the party venue but know I must be close when I see both Ed Miliband and Mariella Frostrup heading in the same direction.

As Mr. Wickham and Lydia Bennet, Louis Partridge and Rhea Norwood prove love-bombing, breadcrumbing, and ghosting are far from modern affectations. Partridge wears a Brunello Cucinelli wool coat. Lemaire shirt. Brioni trousers. Vintage cravat from Costume Studio. Norwood wears a McQueen silk dress with chain detail. Top, stylist’s own.

Olivia and Rufus doing some fantastic drunk acting today. Mischievous and silly. Lisa tells a story about an actor who insisted on getting so pissed for a drunk scene that he scared the make-up crew and kept sending unit drivers out to get more booze. Finally Lisa said to him exasperatedly, “Can’t you just act it?”

Jamie’s on fine Collins form today, adding all sorts of awkward noises into his scenes. He keeps making Hollie get the giggles, and Hollie has the most infectious laugh I’ve ever heard so it sets everyone off.

Sniffing around Jamie to get the tea on Charli xcx’s wedding but he is annoyingly classy and discreet.

Emma and Jack’s first kissing scene. I really don’t know how actors do this stone-cold sober in the broad light of day. There was a lot of discussion about whether they would have kissed in this scene. As my historical advisor Dr. Fiona Stafford once sagely said to me during scripting, “They would have had all the same desires as us.” Jack and Emma ultimately decide it is the right moment for Darcy and Lizzy to kiss. “They’d be gantin’ for it,” Jack says. I laugh. “Sorry,” he says. “The Irish are romantics, the Scottish are pragmatic.”

At one point, Euros calls out to Emma: “Emma, slightly adjust your spencer,” referring to the short jackets women wore in Georgian England.

“Oh,” he says, still looking puzzled. “As in ‘Marks & ’?”

Fiona is giving it some real welly today in Lady Catherine’s crowning scene. Terrifying. Golden leaves on all trees. Emma, Will, and Laura will not stop talking about The Celebrity Traitors despite me telling them that I have not yet watched it on catch-up.

Austen-mania has revved up again (does it ever rev down?) because Andrew Davies has announced he’s going to bring out the darker elements of Emma and Mansfield Park in new adaptations. The Today programme has asked if I want to come on and talk about it, but I’ve decided I’m not going to say anything about Austen until the show is out, otherwise everyone will be utterly sick of me.

Daryl is complimentary about my new perfume, which I will also write about in my own private diary, possibly in a pink glitter gel pen.

Jack does another non-speaking scene today in which he has to do lots of takes looking intrigued and deep in thought, and some takes where he looks intrigued and beguiled, so we have options. He laughs on his 10th take: “God, this is a silly job isn’t it?”

Mavor and Daryl McCormack: a Jane and Bingley for the ages. “I wish boys dressed like this now,” writes Alderton wistfully of McCormack’s breaches on set. Mavor wears a Ralph Lauren Collection velvet dress. Rachel Boston earrings and pendant necklace. McCormack wears wool tailcoat, cotton shirt, pleated satin collar, and wool trousers, all from Dior.

Head to the O2 to watch Little Simz in the Netflix box. I love Little Simz and have never seen her live, so am mega excited. Even happier to get there and see all the Bennet sisters draining the free bar, although strange for them to be not in corsets. Even stranger to watch them dancing to hip-hop. Emma (whose dialogue was sampled on Little Simz’s album Sometimes I Might Be Introvert) opens the show with the song they featured on. They march down the stage looking phenomenally cool in a pinstripe brown suit, performing their lines. We all scream and cheer until we are hoarse.

I ask Alice (Netflix executive producer) nosey questions about her love life, give unwarranted advice, and list various men I could set her up with. Am reminded of something my agent Clare once said: “At some point, a woman discovers that there is a Mrs.

Land early at Heathrow from LA where I’ve been for a week and head straight to set for the proposal scene. I’m so happy to be back in cold, crisp, glorious English countryside in my big sheepskin coat. Olivia got everyone a waffle truck as a present.

For some reason, any time Lizzy runs, it feels too modern. I don’t know why. It’s hard to do period running. Those jogging arms feel like such a 20th century invention. After a few goes, they find the right Lizzy gait and it looks natural.

The proposal is perfect. I’m so glad I get to witness it behind a monitor, cup of tea in hand. Big silent sobs from me today. We are so, so lucky to have Jack and Emma.

Did some nice milling around and chatting at unit base with Jack and Rufus. Ask them about their most embarrassing pap moment. Jack says he was recently followed by a photographer when he was running in a park and became so self-conscious he panicked and did a “made-up stretch.” Rufus says he was photographed buying a frying pan which somehow became a headline.

Jamie’s last day. Sad to lose him and sad to lose his Collins. Both make me laugh so much, although I only want to have a pint with one of them. I give him his wrap present—a walnut cigarette case stuffed with Marlboro Golds. I thought it was a Regency gentleman present until I googled it and realised that cigarette cases were a Victorian invention. This is the refrain of my entire time researching historical details for the show. Almost everything we recognise now, the Victorians invented. Maybe Dickens next.

As Charlotte Lucas and Mr. Collins, Jasmine Blackborow and Jamie Demetriou have some tricks up their sleeves. Improvising Regency conversation? Simply ask, “Is your father fond of horses?” Blackborow wears a vintage jacquard corset and velvet hat from Rellik. Ermanno Scervino blouse and trousers. Stephen Jones veiled headband. Sophie Bille Brahe pearl earrings. Demetriou wears an Issey Miyake trench coat and trousers. Vintage shirt and cravat from Costume Studio.

Filming the Meryton Assembly. Mortifying moment when I think Jack is waving at me really excitedly from behind a glass door and I wave back with equal enthusiasm, only to realise he is trying to get someone’s attention because he’d been locked in a vestibule and is needed on set.

I’ve broken my finger from pushing a child on the playground swings too vigorously (child known to me, not random child). Child fine. Four hours waiting in A&E for me to be told there’s nothing they can do but bind it and send me to the “specialist hand clinic” in Archway. Pat (set PA) tells me he broke his finger once and had to get screws put into his hand and shows me the X-ray. I think I’m being quietly dignified about the whole thing, until Lisa tells me, “There’s no point suffering in silence unless everybody knows about it.”

Bree’s last day. She barks on demand like a pro. “She’s always on her lines,” Lisa observes. We all clap her off as she trots off with her handler.

It’s suddenly turned bitingly cold and everyone’s wearing long johns under their jeans. Freya’s on her hobby horse again. We’ve had to reshoot some of it because in the last take, she looked like a jockey at Aintree for some reason.

Snow at Longbourn! I cannot believe it! Thank God the crew were all here. At about 7am, before we’d started shooting, it suddenly bucketed down with snow. The type of snow you don’t get in England—thick and blanket-y. The crew ran outside and filmed it all. It’s probably saved us tens of thousands of pounds in visual effects for the winter episode.

In a perfect twist of fate, today’s our Christmas lunch and we’re all in Christmas jumpers. Christmas music blasts from the catering vans and our plates are loaded up with roast potatoes, roast beef, brussels, gravy, and cauliflower cheese (I think you really need the cauliflower cheese in a Christmas lunch and I’m not interested in debating it).

Very emotional goodbyes with the Bennet girls. I leave their wrap presents and cards in all of their trailers—an old black and white photo of the Golden Parsonage in a gold frame, so they’ll always have a piece of Longbourn. This loud, chaotic, special place that really had felt like our home for the last few months.

There is such a sadness and such an intimacy to these last days of a production. As you wind down, you gradually say goodbye to all the members of the cast until eventually there’s only one or two of them left. Only Olivia and Emma remain, and they’re doing their most emotional scene today. It was scheduled well, as they’re now holding the entire history of their characters’ stories in their heads, which massively enriches the emotion of their performances. More sobbing from me. Sobbing from all of us, actually.

Sad to say goodbye to Olivia, who has been an absolute joy on set. Always mucking in and being helpful. I know that’s the thing everyone says about her, so it feels so clichéd and luvvy-ish even typing it, but it’s true.

“Jack and Emma’s performances are beautiful,” writes Alderton. “Halting, delicate, vulnerable. It works particularly well in the vast grandeur of the surroundings.” Lowden wears a Loro Piana cashmere coat and tweed waistcoat. Favourbrook shirt. Brunello Cucinelli trousers. Vintage cravat from Costume Studio. Cufflinks, stylist’s own. Emma wears a Miu Miu minidress. Phoebe English sheer shirt. Ermanno Scervino lace-trimmed skirt. Calzedonia tights. Neous slingbacks. Jewelry, as before.

I ask Emma if they mind that they’re spending their last day without any other cast. We’re filming lots of Lizzy walking on her own. They say it feels right, as so much of the show has been Lizzy trudging through the countryside. Emma likes that they’re ending as we began—the cameras following Lizzy on her own journey.

Emma really has held up the whole show. They’ve been in almost every day of the shoot and they always have so much energy, a smile for everyone; they’re always on their lines. They’ve never complained, even when they were so cold in the Peak District and had to walk around with a hot water bottle attached to them the next day. They’ve deep-dived into the book and embodied Lizzy so fully. A class act in every single sense.

Euros is presented with his wrap gift from the crew—they’ve secretly plotted with his husband to restore his old trombone back to its former glory. He is so delighted and surprised. Hoping for a performance at the wrap party.

It’s a cold and clear day and Will and I stand shivering in the middle of a field for Emma’s last scene—a tracking shot of Lizzy running. We do a few takes then Chris (first assistant director) bellows the sentence I’ve been dreading since we started: “That is a wrap on Pride and Prejudice.” I run over to Emma and squeeze the life out of them. “I’m so proud of you,” I say. “I’m so proud of you,” they reply. We’re both in tears. Lisa sidles over and tells us to pull ourselves together.

Well. Nearly. Just 10 months of editing ahead…

Pride and Prejudice is on Netflix December 3.

#6494. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6493. This Clever Fork Trick Makes Slicing Cheese So Much Easier

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

As much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

One of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

#6492. Why ‘Blackout Wednesday’ Has Become One Of The Biggest Drinking Nights Of The Year

Thanksgiving Eve is fun and nostalgic—but it can turn risky fast.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different. Most people have the next day off, and college students or young professionals are typically back in their hometowns for the holiday. What better way to kick off the long weekend than to get off your parents’ couch and hit up the local watering hole?

That’s how Thanksgiving Eve came to be known as “Blackout Wednesday” or “Drinksgiving,” one of the busiest drinking nights of the year. A 2023 study found that in 2022, liquor sales grew by 156% and beer sales increased by 85% on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Cocktail orders surged by 69%.

DoorDash has even named the day one of the busiest for alcohol deliveries. Among 10 more traditional holidays like New Year’s Eve and July 4th, Blackout Wednesday ranks right in the middle. “As families and friends return home for the winter holidays, the day before Thanksgiving has become the fifth most popular day for alcohol delivery,” DoorDash’s website reads.

Going out in your hometown is prime time for idly snooping on people from high school, witnessing some truly unlikely pairings (Tyler and Kayla?!). It’s social and nostalgic, but it’s also a day when one drink can easily turn into one too many.

It’s not all fun and drinking games, however. This unofficial holiday marks the start of so-called “DUI Season,” with checkpoints ramping up before Turkey Day. Your risk of coming into contact with a drunk driver also becomes 55% higher than on average days.

Short-term risks of heavy drinking and blacking out include vomiting, seizures, depression, and accidental injuries, as well as next-day anxiety and depression. Long-term, recurring binges are linked to liver damage, high blood pressure, and mental health issues. Alcohol-induced blackouts can also occur more rapidly after just a few drinks, especially if you are taking certain medications, drink on an empty stomach, or have a low body weight.

It’s totally valid to blow off some steam (or get out of chopping celery), just plan it smart. With actually-delicious mocktails, non-alcoholic beers, and ride-shares, there’s very little reason to put yourself—or others—in danger, especially during the holidays.

Hosts and guests alike can benefit from making a plan for keeping everyone safe until well after New Year’s Day by providing plenty of non-alcoholic options at gatherings, opting in on a “Dampsgiving,” checking in with loved ones (and designated drivers) before they hit the road, and always making sure there’s a spot on the couch for anyone who helped themselves to a few too many eggnog espresso martinis.

#6491. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6490. Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

For the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:

I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a big deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really important to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

#6488. The Ideal Thanksgiving Place Setting for Every Member of the Family

The only thing that feels more like Thanksgiving than an exquisitely burnished roast turkey is the (sometimes chaotic) assemblage of loved ones seated around it. For your tablescape this year, take inspiration from the beautifully unique cast of characters that make a family a family.

She just stepped off a red eye from the big city, but she looks like she came from a gallery opening—and her place setting is as bold and eclectic as her fashion sense. Bulbous postmodern ceramic plates, '90s Art Deco revival flatware from Japan, and a hand-beaded placemat are exactly the things she’d be into. The button-shaped aluminum coaster is seldom occupied, since she prefers to keep the martini glass right where it belongs: in her hand.

She’s 25 going on 70. In between baking all of the pies for the big dinner, she learned lace-making from a TikTok tutorial. She sews, she antiques, and she self-publishes Jane Austen fanfic online. The cheeky cotton bottle apron and pearl-tipped doily on her table might be brand new from Gohar World, but they pair exquisitely with the pewter flatware she scored at an estate sale. Quilted floral placemats and plates adorned with dainty, hand-painted bows from The Six Bells, a store leading the revival of country cottage decor, evoke the pastoral, bucolic lifestyle she yearns for (as long as she can keep her 10-step skin-care routine).

Herzerlmuster Scalloped Placemats (Set of 2)

The combo of unbridled energy and still-developing motor skills means the Gen-Alpha kids are best served by a spread of disposable and shatterproof items. And, seeing that it’ll take some clever coaxing to pull these little gremlins away from their screens, their table must match the intense digital stimuli they’re accustomed to. Loop-de-loop silly straws, melamine plates, and acrylic forks and cups in as many colors as possible are the bare minimum to keep minds forged in a Cocomelon crucible engaged for the total duration of a Thanksgiving meal. Despite the visual chaos, their table might be more tranquil than the adults’.

Prue Leith Melamine Dinnerware Set and Tumblers

Thanksgiving might be the only time you see this elusive individual, as he otherwise spends the year fussing around his DIY Earthship in the desert outside of Santa Fe. His place setting is filled with natural materials, like these Shigaraki-style earthenware plates and zero-waste Belgian linen placemats. If he starts defending his dedication to composting toilets a little too enthusiastically, fill his hand-carved wooden mug with some herbal tea and he’ll settle down fine.

A matriarch par excellence, she’s been holding the family together for decades. Her demeanor might be as breezy as a Big Sur afternoon, but she means business when it comes to hosting Thanksgiving. Let it be known: She had a Nancy Meyers kitchen long before Nancy Meyers picked up a camera. To steal her vibe, invest in an Italian table cloth festooned with vines, hand-painted ceramic wicker plates, and bamboo-stemmed wine glasses. Place cards, arranged for maximum harmony, should bear each name in handwritten cursive. Miss Manners would be so proud.

#6487. White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

The nutritional showdown nobody asked for—but everyone at Thanksgiving needs.

Every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps. There's Team White Meat, politely asking for "just a slice of breast, please." Then there's Team Dark Meat, already eyeing the drumstick like it's the last Pop-Tart in the box. It's basically Team Edward vs. Team Jacob, but with gravy.

Somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice. As a dietitian, I get asked about this a lot, especially the week of Thanksgiving. The short answer is that dark meat isn't the villain it's made out to be. The long answer is way more interesting, so grab a fork. Cranberry sauce optional.

The color comes down to a protein called myoglobin. Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle cells, and muscles that work steadily over long periods need more of it. On a turkey, that means the legs and thighs, which the bird uses to stand and walk around all day.

Domestic turkeys use their breast muscles far less, so they carry less myoglobin and stay pale. Myoglobin contains heme iron, which matters for nutrition. More on that in a minute.

So when you choose dark meat, you're eating hardworking muscle. That changes its nutritional profile in a few notable ways.

Both cuts are excellent sources of protein. A 3-ounce serving of roasted, skinless turkey provides roughly 24 to 25 grams of protein, whether it's white or dark meat. White meat edges ahead by a gram or two, but in practical terms, both will do the job.

If protein is a priority, either cut gets you there. No need to stage a dramatic family intervention over the drumsticks.

Skinless dark meat does have more fat than skinless white meat, typically a few extra grams per 3-ounce serving. Some of that is saturated fat.

Context matters, though. The difference amounts to a few grams on a single plate, not a massive gap. Keeping the skin on also adds more fat to either cut. A slice of breast with crispy skin can end up in a similar ballpark to skinless thigh meat.

Saturated fat and heart health remain an active area of research. A Cochrane systematic review found that reducing dietary saturated fat was linked to a modest reduction in cardiovascular events over time. That finding reflects overall eating patterns across months and years, though, not what you eat at one holiday meal. A few extra grams of fat from turkey thighs won't make or break anyone's health.

Fat also brings flavor and moisture, which is why dark meat rarely turns into the dry, sawdust situation that can happen to an overcooked breast.

Remember myoglobin? Thanks in part to its heme iron, dark meat generally contains more iron than white meat. Heme iron, the type found in animal foods, is generally absorbed more efficiently than the non-heme iron found in plants.

That's meaningful, because iron deficiency is the most common cause of anemia worldwide. It's especially common among people who menstruate, pregnant people, and young children. Turkey thighs won't fix a deficiency on their own, but they can absolutely contribute to your overall iron intake.

Dark meat also delivers noticeably more zinc than white meat. Zinc plays a key role in immune function, wound healing, and taste perception. Not bad for the part of the bird some people skip.

This is where things get fun, because each cut has its own nutritional strengths.

These B vitamins help your body turn food into usable energy. Vitamin B12 also supports nerve function and red blood cell production, and B12 deficiency is more common in older adults and people who eat few animal foods.

Neither cut offers a complete B vitamin package on its own. Together, though? They make a pretty great team.

Not really. It's just different. White meat offers slightly more protein and less fat, plus more niacin and B6. Dark meat has more iron, zinc, and riboflavin, plus richer flavor and a juicier texture. Both provide vitamin B12.

Neither one deserves a "good" or "bad" label. Health is shaped by your eating patterns over time, not by which slice you pick from the platter on one Thursday in November.

If you have a specific health condition, a registered dietitian can help you figure out what works best for you. For most people, though, the best turkey is the one you actually enjoy eating.

Pick the cut you love. Better yet, take a little of both. Dark meat isn't a nutritional compromise, and white meat isn't a punishment. They're two parts of the same bird, each with its own strengths.

So go ahead and claim that drumstick. Or the breast. Or both. Your plate, your call. Just save some gravy for the rest of us.

#6486. Giant Sheet-Pan Chocolate Almond Croissant

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

This giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

Bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

Meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

Sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

Yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

Yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

Serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

#6485. Shannon Abloh Opens Up About Virgil Abloh’s Legacy, Five Years After His Death

Shannon Abloh and her two children, Lowe, 13, and Grey, 10, usually mark the birthday of her late husband, the designer Virgil Abloh, at their home in Chicago. They order cupcakes from Virgil’s favorite local bakery—his preferred flavor: vanilla with vanilla frosting. They talk about their memories and write them down in a notebook.

Shannon has not been eager to speak personally about Virgil—she’s given few interviews since his death five years ago. But if anything, his life and mission—to create a startling new vocabulary for fashion that speaks to those who have too often been sidelined—only seems more radical now. And on today of all days she feels permission to talk about him. “I think it was a nod from him,” she tells me when I appear at the house on his birthday, September 30 (the only date our schedules aligned for an interview). “It was a sign; it was him saying, ‘It’s okay. You can do this. You are the one to talk about me. You are the one that is doing this work.’ ” Part of that work is bringing “Virgil Abloh: The Codes,” the exhibition that opened in Paris last fall with nearly 1,000 objects from his archive, to The Shed, the massive performance and curatorial space on Manhattan’s West Side. And there’s Shannon’s own account of living with grief half a decade after Virgil’s death. She hopes that her story might reach someone going through something similar.

Spread across multiple lots in a quiet Lincoln Park neighborhood, the fortress-like home has the muffled quiet of a well-insulated studio—there is, actually, a makeshift studio in the basement with a very small drum set that once belonged to Grey and vintage turntables, a casual shrine to Virgil’s DJ’ing days and the tables he installed in his offices at Louis Vuitton after he was appointed artistic director there in 2018. Near the entryway, a skate­boarding ramp Virgil designed—made of bronze but molded to look like plywood, a characteristic high-low mixture of materials—has been transformed into a bench.

A cocoon-like softness extends throughout the house—​the curtains, the upholstery, the carpets are mostly in muted colors: dove gray, cream, lilac, an occasional pop of violet. A wall of windows frames the backyard, where smoke- and rose-​colored quartz crystals—​sourced from a convention in Arizona that Shannon’s friend brought her to—sit like small boulders. Wisteria is climbing the drainpipe, raindrops streaming from its leaves and flowers.

As we settle into Shannon’s study, she speeds through the early years of their relationship. She and Virgil met when they were teenagers—attending different high schools in Rockford, Illinois—at the indoor soccer game of a mutual friend. He later left flowers on her car with a note explaining that he would be a good boyfriend. “And that was it,” she tells me, with Midwestern matter-​of-​factness. “I was like, ‘Sure, okay.’ ”

He wasn’t popular in the stereotypical sense of the word, she says, but “everybody knew who he was” and he veered easily between the tribal cohorts of high school. And Shannon knew, too, that there was something extraordinary between them. “When he left for college,” she remembers, “I was just like, Oh, this is definitely my person.”

Shannon ended up at Eastern Illinois University outside of Champaign—far from the cityscapes familiar to her, and even farther from Virgil, who was attending the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “I knew I needed to change my life,” she says, and so she transferred to a small school in Madison. Virgil was then studying to be a civil engineer, carting his vinyl to gigs in Shannon’s Nissan Pathfinder, partying but never drinking. “He could walk into any room and know someone,” says Shannon. His final year in college, he took an art history course, and, as Shannon tells it, the class ignited something. “He figured out who Caravaggio was.”

WALKING THE WALK The Abloh family in Chicago, the city Shannon and Virgil settled in after college.

Virgil and Shannon both moved separately to Chicago after college, where Virgil studied architecture at Illinois Institute of Technology and Shannon worked in marketing, includinga stint at Yahoo. Virgil would come to the apartment Shannon shared with two of her friends almost every night, typing away on the big desktop computer in their living room while they made plans for the evening. “That rhythm of Virgil in 1999 was the same rhythm of Virgil at the height of his career,” says one of those early roommates, Marcie Pistol Haley, who now works for Virgil Abloh Securities, the entity that oversees projects tied to his name. A chance encounter led him to someone who worked for Kanye West, and Virgil was appointed West’s creative director in 2002. “I saw this fire in his eyes when he started,” says Shannon. “Like: This is real. I can turn this into a career.”

By the time Shannon and Virgil were engaged in 2008, they had been together for 10 years, and as Virgil’s work accelerated, they began to settle into certain roles. He was the outward-​oriented best-​friend-​to-​everyone; she was the private foundation of their union. At home, though, she was an integral part of his creative process. “When he started his first collection, Pyrex”—the short-​lived precursor to Off-White—“I was sitting on the floor, pricing out the clothing,” says Shannon.She “knew everything that was on his mind,” says Athiththan Selvendran, who was Virgil’s assistant from 2016 onward and now also works for Virgil Abloh Securities. “She was his sounding board.” Sometimes Virgil would bring home things for Shannon to try on that she was less enthused about. “I would be like, ‘Really?’ ” she remembers. “And he’s like, ‘Yes, you have to just rock it.’ I was like, ‘Okay.’ ”

The two were married in 2009, moving into the Bucktown neighborhood in Chicago. A few years later, in 2013—​the same year that Virgil launched Off-White—​Lowe was born, and then Grey followed in 2016. At the same time, Virgil was opening concept stores in Tokyo, spinning out collaborations with Takashi Murakami at Gagosian, pushing sneakerhead culture to new heights through a lauded collaboration with Nike, earning the double-edged honor of being one of the only Black men to lead a heritage fashion house, and, as many would tell it, doing more than anyone else to legitimize streetwear as high fashion. “He traveled 300 days out of the year,” says Selvendran. “He went out and he DJ’d and he did everything,” says his friend former Dior Men designer Kim Jones, who worked with Virgil under Kanye West. “I was like, How many Virgils are there?”

Some would take a more critical view of all this frenetic activity. There was his lack of formal fashion training: “The clothes fit his models,” was the faint praise offered by The Washington Post’s Robin Givhan after an Off-White show in 2017. People put Virgil “in the bracket of non-​designer,” says Jones, who preceded Virgil at Vuitton as menswear artistic director. And hype could seem like an end in itself: “To me, they are on the same level as a sculpture of David or the Mona Lisa,” Virgil once said of his deconstructed Nikes. But, adds Jones, “some people who were quite negative about what Virgil did have become very positive about it. They can see what it means to the generation of now.” The criticism may have even fed Off-White’s reputation: “The more criticism that he got, the more sweaters we sold,” says Edward Buchanan, a knitwear designer who worked for Virgil at Off-White and now runs a hub for Black creatives in Milan.

Shannon, who had stopped working when her daughter was born, saw her part in his career with firm but dispassionate clarity. She would simply get out the stroller when Virgil had to abruptly fly off, and she’d take her children to her parents’ house in Chicago. Up to this point in the conversation, Shannon has been composed, but as she pulls her legs up under her on the sofa to describe their years as a young family, her voice trembles. “He had big dreams,” she says. “Telling him he needed to stay home in Chicago and be with the kids—that wouldn’t make him happy. I knew being a dad was incredibly important to him, but so was his work.” The family sometimes tagged along—to fashion shows or the Louis Vuitton headquarters in Paris. Lowe was visiting him at the LV office one day when she was six or seven and made a purse out of paper. “And then Virgil gave it to someone and was like, ‘Make this into a bag,’ ” Shannon says. The designer’s mission to democratize design was not only about production and distribution but instilling the idea of capability: If you think it, you can build it.

Late in the summer of 2019, he started to feel run-​down, unable to recover, even when he broke with routine and took time to rest. A series of tests revealed that he had cardiac angiosarcoma, a rare, aggressive cancer that starts in the heart. It was very important to Virgil that only a very small number of people knew what was really going on. “He didn’t want the first question everyone asked him to be ‘Are you okay?’ ” Shannon says. And so it was just his immediate family, and maybe one or two friends, who knew the truth—which was not always easy for his wife: “I’m someone that needs to talk about things, but those were his wishes, and so I had to respect that. There were definitely moments where I felt like it could have been better if we had opened up our circle a little bit more, but he just didn’t want people to worry about him.”

New demands took over Virgil and Shannon’s life. They started flying to Houston’s MD Anderson Hospital to see a specialist. “Having his doctor so far away was nerve-​racking,” says Shannon, “but having it separated from our daily life was also a bit of a reprieve. When we left Houston, it was kind of like, Okay, we have however long until we have to be back here for scans or chemo or surgery.”

During the pandemic the family burrowed inward. It was an eerily beautiful time, Shannon says, when the children got to have their father at home. They decamped to the Ablohs’ house in Wisconsin’s Lake Geneva, where the kids would play soccer in the yard or hunt for frogs in the pond on the property. Grey was young, but Virgil was teaching him to skateboard, and he would make and decorate paper airplanes for his children that Shannon has kept to this day.

The couple never fought—they just weren’t the kind of people who could sustain confrontation, Shannon says—but she began to see a darker side of her exuberant husband. “He was angry. He struggled with thoughts of ‘What did I do to deserve something like this?’ ” she remembers. Virgil started seeing a therapist. (Shannon sees the same person now, which she describes as oddly comforting: “She doesn’t share details, but she’ll be like, ‘Oh, we actually talked about this.’ And it’s reassuring that it’s like, Okay, Virgil and I are thinking similarly.”)

When Virgil died on November 28, 2021, there was the initial wallop of grief, the world-tilting disorientation. Shannon recalls a trip to the supermarket that elicited fury: “I’m like, None of these people know that my person died. I’m standing here in the checkout line and everybody else is fine, and my person is gone and that’s not fair.” Old-fashioned mourning dress would be helpful, she remembers thinking—an outward sign of an inward destruction.

There was also a barrage of questions. Few plans existed, Shannon says, for Virgil’s many projects, the scheduled collaborations, a forthcoming book. “Virgil made everyone feel like they were the most important person in the room,” Shannon says—a blessing for those in his orbit, and a burden to the person being asked to continue that affirmation in the midst of a personal tragedy. She had always felt secure in the background and in the knowledge that she, and his children, actually were the most important people in his life. But after his death she found herself pushed to the fore: “Everyone looked at me and they’re like, ‘He told me that we were going to do this project, and here it is, and can I continue it?’ ” At first Shannon just waved the projects through. But after a few months, that began to feel wrong. “And that’s when I went into my shell and just started saying no to everything. It didn’t make a lot of people very happy.”

HANGING IN Shannon, left with Lowe and Grey, has been involved in the work of the The Virgil Abloh Foundation. “It was just a place for me to start to put one foot in front of the other,” she says.

We move to her kitchen, where Shannon’s assistant, Evelyn, has set out sandwiches and a salad on a capacious and spotless counter. As we sit, she begins to tell me about her reentry. A little over a year after Virgil’s death, Shannon felt able to convene what she calls a “summit” to decide how to carry on his larger mission. She also had to consider her place in it all—on the rare occasion she would speak at events, she would often find herself tearing up offstage while clips of Virgil’s voice played, then having to take the stage with mascara running down her face. “She definitely did not ask to or want to ever hold this torch,” says Pistol Haley. But Shannon also felt she had to do something.

Perhaps, when Shannon took the helm of Virgil Abloh Securities—the “creative corporation” conceived of by Virgil before his death—she sensed that Off-White’s future would be uncertain without its charismatic leader. “He was the voice of Off-White,” says Jones. “So it sounded different without him there.” Or Shannon might have just realized that she had little control over what happened to the brand: At the time of Virgil’s death, LVMH owned 60 percent of Off-White. While there was something of a comeback show at New York Fashion Week in 2024, staged by Virgil’s successor, IB Kamara, LVMH subsequently sold Off-White to Bluestar Alliance—a self-described “brand management company” that owns mall stalwarts like Limited Too and Brookstone. The deal seemed to imply a less glorious future for Off-White than high-profile runway shows. Earlier this year, Kamara left the brand. “Off-White was still a young company,” Buchanan points out. “Without Virgil being there to distinguish how he wanted things to move into the future—just the vision was very different.” In our very first call, Shannon tells me she doesn’t want to get into the fate or trajectory of Off-White.

Shannon did want to perpetuate Virgil’s ideals around diversity and representation, however. In 2025 the Virgil Abloh Foundation launched a program that mentors and guides Chicago teenagers, offering them opportunities for cultural connection and exposure—taking the inaugural class to Paris and the subsequent class to Italy. The organization convened the third group this fall, and they will go to New York in December to see “The Codes” and then to London for spring break. This work and the foundation, more broadly, are “part of my grief work,” Shannon says. “It was just a place for me to start to put one foot in front of the other.”

It’s raining when I leave the house, and the neighborhood is quiet. Suddenly, a rush of teenagers dismissed from school fills the streets. They cling to each other’s hips and hold sweatshirts over their heads—rough and gentle with each other, ebullient and moody. The electricity and possibility is palpable among these kids, with their whole lives ahead of them.

#6484. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6482. I Tried Ina Garten’s Ranch Dressing, and It Changed My Mind About Ranch

I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

Add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

That’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is important, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

The first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

And the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

In her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

By the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making plans for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.
