#6481. Citrus Madeleines

Marcel Proust and madeleines are so intrinsically linked that in France, a madeleine de Proust has become a common expression used to describe a smell, sound, or taste that brings back old memories. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

As much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

Put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy.

Sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside.

Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy.

Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined.

Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight.

Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour.

Use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour.

Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C.

Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly.

Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.

#6479. Dirty Martini Latkes

If your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

The latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

#6478. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6477. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin

No ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

My kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

#6475. Striped Malted Pound Cake

My earliest dessert obsession was the malted milkshake, which I indulged in every time I had enough babysitting money. My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

This cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

More delicious loaf cake recipes this way.

Grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess.

In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder.

In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice.

On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated.

Add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using).

Transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter.

To create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula.

Place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes.

Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

In a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes.

Remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

#6474. Sheet-Pan Thanksgiving Dinner

Whether you're hosting a small gathering this year or simply craving the comforting flavors of Thanksgiving any time of year, this sheet-pan dinner is the way to go. It’s a feast that’s as cozy as it is convenient, bringing together the classics with a few flavorful twists. The beauty of this meal lies in its simplicity—everything roasts together on a single pan, making cleanup a breeze.

The turkey:Using a bone-in split turkey breast helps ensure juicy, flavorful meat with rich, golden skin, slathered with butter and seasoned with poultry seasoning. This nod to tradition is enhanced with a touch of smoky paprika and garlic to amp up the flavors. For the stuffing, I went the classic route, using store-bought seasoned cubes for a bit of nostalgia, along with onions, celery, and soy sauce to boost the savory notes, and cranberries for a hint of sweetness. The stuffing offers the best of both worlds, with crispy edges and an irresistibly savory center soaked in turkey drippings.

The sweet potatoes:The sweet potatoes strike a perfect balance, spiced with warm and aromatic garam masala—a perfect pairing with the sweet yet earthy tuber. A splash of orange juice adds a tart-sweet touch, while pecans provide a satisfying crunch. If garam masala isn’t your thing, a dash of pumpkin pie spice works beautifully.

The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

Make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. The stuffing can be made a day ahead; just be sure to cool it completely before refrigerating. Even the turkey can be buttered and seasoned the day before, leaving you with just the assembly and roasting on the day of.

#6473. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Hold the jelly! The iconic peanut butter brand is taking a surprisingly savory direction with its latest product.

Who says peanut butter doesn’t deserve a spot in your dinner rotation?

Jif, the beloved peanut butter brand that’s been a staple in American pantries for decades, has ventured into some unexpected territory. If you’re a frequent Costco shopper, you might want to take a closer look the next time you’re browsing the instant noodles.

Rather than replicating the sweet, creamy taste of a spoonful of peanut butter, the noodles take a more savory approach. The seasoning contains peanut flour alongside ingredients like soy sauce, garlic and artificial beef flavor.

As always, product availability can vary by warehouse, so it’s worth checking your warehouse’s stock online before making a special trip. You can also buy the Jif instant ramen at Walmart or Amazon.

But the real question is, would you give peanut butter ramen a try, or is this one food crossover you’ll happily sit out?

#6469. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease.

The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes.

Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. This form of immune memory, known as "trained immunity," broadly enhances the cells' defenses, enabling them to respond to threats more quickly and powerfully than "untrained" cells would.

To flip that switch in the cells, a molecule latches onto the spool that DNA is wound around, specifically near genes involved in sparking inflammation. That subtle molecular tweak "holds those genes poised for rapid activation," said Musa Mhlanga, a cell biologist and molecular geneticist at the Radboud Institute for Molecular Life Sciences in the Netherlands who wasn't involved in the new study.

However, scientists didn't know how that change was maintained over time.

The immune memory should have been destroyed soon after it was made, given that "the cell has enzymes whose entire job is to strip that mark off," Mhlanga told Live Science in an email. But somehow, the memory stuck. "So the obvious question was never really answered: how does a mark survive weeks or months against machinery actively removing it?" Mhlanga said.

The research focused on cells of the innate immune system, including macrophages (pictured), which gobble up germs, dead cells and cellular debris.

The new study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Science Immunology, may answer that question.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The research investigated the phenomenon in mouse immune cells and live lab mice, as well as some human cells in lab dishes. Past studies hinted that, when immune cells switch into their "primed" state, their metabolism changes. This, in turn, drives up the production of a molecule called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which has long been known to help regulate how DNA gets packaged in cells.

In this case, though, the molecule took on a surprising role, Mhlanga said. NAD+ usually gets used up when enzymes orchestrate chemical reactions. But when it comes to the enzymes that normally erase immune cells' memory, called KDM5a, that wasn't the case.

NAD+ latches onto that epigenetic eraser but doesn't get used up in the process; instead, it shuts down KDM5a, as if it were pushing an "off" button. By restraining its memory eraser, the immune cell remains in a primed and activated state, ready to ignite inflammation when triggered.

In experiments with mice, the researchers found that reducing or eliminating NAD+ from immune cells prevented them from entering this primed state. In mice with cancer, this hobbled the immune system's ability to attack tumor cells.

Additionally, in aging mice, the team observed that NAD+ levels dwindle in concert with the innate immune system's ability to respond to threats. The research builds a convincing "molecular bridge" between those two facts, Mhlanga said, raising a hypothesis for why immunity gets worse with age.

Broadly, the research adds to scientists' understanding of how innate immune cells enter this primed, inflammatory state. This line of research may help scientists understand "why some vaccines protect against diseases they were never designed for," Mhlanga said.

For example, a tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BDG) is thought to mount a broad immune response that may help stave off many conditions, from viral infections to Alzheimer's disease. (Some scientists think that Alzheimer's stems from a dysregulated immune response that BCG may help to normalize.)

While this line of research could have wide-ranging applications, the new study has some limitations. The researchers did a few experiments with human cells and backed up some of their findings in mice with data from human cancer patients. However, "the human data are thin by comparison with the mouse work," Mhlanga noted, so they bear further confirmation.

In the future, he'd be interested in studies exploring NAD+ in the context of the aging immune system, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The recent research hints that pushing NAD+ to optimal levels could help counter each of these conditions.

But especially in cancer, where the disease's biology varies by the tumour type and stage, "it is not a simple 'more NAD+ is better' story," he cautioned, "and I'd resist it being written as one."

#6462. Homemade Turkey Stock

Turkey stock is a must-make if you had turkey as your Thanksgiving centerpiece. You don't want to let those scraps go to waste, do you? Throw in some of those wilting herbs and whatever carrots and celery you have on hand to make a great pantry staple. It takes almost zero effort and leaves you with a flavorful stock that you can store in the freezer until you're ready to put it to use.

You can make basically anything you'd make with chicken stock (which is a lot!) with this stock. One of the best uses of turkey stock is turkey gravy and that can be used to top something like poutine or stuffing. Or you can make a time-tested classic Turkey Tetrazzini. Whatever you do, don't let this stock go to waste.

Add all of the ingredients to a large stockpot. Cover turkey completely with water, about 10 to 12 cups.

Over medium heat, bring the stockpot to a boil, then reduce heat and let it simmer for 3 hours. Spoon fat off the top as it rises.

Strain stock through a fine mesh strainer. Let the stock cool to room temperature.

Store in refrigerator until ready to use for up to 2 weeks or in the freezer for 3 months.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Stock is the perfect thing to store in your freezer! After letting your stock cool to room temp you can store in the refrigerator for 2 weeks or in the freezer for up to 3 months. Set it out in the fridge the night before you plan to use to defrost or place it in a pan of barely simmering water to thaw out quickly!

#6461. Why Pizza Has Become an Unofficial Thanksgiving Tradition

Turkey gets Thursday, but Wednesday is all about the 'za.

It’s Thanksgiving Eve. The turkey is hogging an entire fridge shelf, every baking dish is spoken for and the cousins just pulled into the driveway. Then somebody asks what’s for dinner, and the only reasonable answer comes in a cardboard box.

If that sounds familiar, you’re in excellent company. As it turns out, the night before the big feast is one of the busiest times of the year for pizza orders, and our collective craving for a good slice is practically a holiday tradition of its own.

Ridiculously popular. According to DoorDash’s latest trends report, pizza was the No. 1 pick this time last year, with orders jumping more than 50% compared with other Wednesdays in November. And the ‘za of choice? Plain cheese, up a whopping 70%.

The craze isn’t limited to the couch, either. Toast data shows that pizza orders at sit-down restaurants and bars spiked 48% that evening. Salads, meanwhile, dipped 5%, which sounds about right.

National chains feel the rush, too. “Across the industry, it consistently lands in the top handful alongside Halloween and the Super Bowl,” Greg Hamilton, chief marketing officer at Little Caesars, said in a statement.

There’s a certain satisfaction in wiping down the counters the day before, knowing the casseroles are assembled and you’re as ready for tomorrow as you’ll ever be. The last thing anyone wants to do is pull another pan out of the cupboard.

“Thanksgiving Eve is about making life easier,” Hamilton said. “The kitchen is already prepped for Thursday, the house is filling up and nobody wants to cook twice.”

But there’s more to it than giving the dishwasher a break. College kids are back in their hometowns, and childhood friends are making plans to reunite. Even siblings who usually communicate via memes in the family group chat are finally in the same room.

With AAA expecting 81.5 million Americans to travel this week, plenty of those reunions kick off a day before anyone carves anything. Order pizza, and whoever’s hosting actually hears the surprise engagement announcement instead of yelling “Wait, WHAT?” over a sizzling skillet.

Most customers “tend to go with the classics,” Hamilton noted, but if you’re looking to shake up your usual order (or feed a small army without spending a fortune), several pizza chains have specials running right now:

Prices and participation vary by location, and given how busy tonight is shaping up to be, ordering ahead isn’t a bad idea.

Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage.

The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science, may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience.

Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech.

In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying ‪—‬ a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia. Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech.

Wernicke's area (red) is found in the left temporal lobe.

But that isn't the whole story. While people who have Wernicke's aphasia can speak in a normal cadence, the words they use don't match their intention. They might substitute semantically related words, with "shoe" becoming "foot," or they might mix up words that have similar sounds, like "leg" and "peg." This can make their sentences sound like nonsensical word salad and thus undermine patients' ability to communicate.

These symptoms make it clear that damage to Wernicke's area affects not just speech comprehension but also speech production. But neuroscientists couldn't identify how this function arose in the brain region or which cells contributed to it.

The question "has remained a mystery for over 150 years now," said study co-author Alexander Silva, a neuroscientist at the University of California, San Francisco.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One hypothesis is [that] it acts kind of like a proofreader. It listens to you speak, and it corrects errors," Silva explained. "But another is that there's actually dedicated activity in this area that generates upcoming speech."

In their new study, Silva and his colleagues set out to solve the conundrum, using a series of complementary tests that involved recording people's brain activity as they spoke. They had access to powerful tools for understanding brain function, like electrocorticography electrodes, which are implanted onto the brain's surface to measure neural activity. The precision of these tools enabled the team to investigate Wernicke's area at high temporal and spatial resolutions, Silva told Live Science.

The team recruited 28 participants with epilepsy, who already had electrodes implanted to monitor their seizures. They identified a small group of brain cells within Wernicke's area that fired about a quarter of a second before participants spoke words aloud. The signal seemed to be preparing for the speech production, and it could be separated from linked auditory signals made by cells responding to the resulting sound of the spoken words.

But this evidence alone couldn't prove that these cells actually caused speech; it could only correlate the signal with speech production. To connect the dots, the scientists mapped the brains of hundreds of people who were undergoing surgery to have temporal-lobe tumors removed and tested how the surgery affected their speech.

This analysis supported their previous findings; patients were much more likely to have trouble speaking after surgery if the procedure had damaged Wernicke's area, suggesting the area had a role in speech production.

We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why.

Finally, in 13 people with implanted electrodes and undamaged Wernicke's areas, the researchers tested what happened when they stimulated the brain. When the scientists sent a wave of electricity through the speech-preparation area just before participants opened their mouths to talk, the stimulation caused them to make word errors that resembled Wernicke's aphasia.

The researchers then moved on to a different question: Could these discoveries about Wernicke's area help people whose speech is affected by brain damage?

Using more electrode data, the team identified individual brain cells in Wernicke's area that were linked to saying particular words. Then, they looked at two patients with speech paralysis; these individuals were unable to speak after strokes damaged their brainstems and they'd had electrodes implanted in their brains that sent signals to brain-computer speech devices.

The devices which interpret signals from undamaged areas of the brain to spell out words the patients are trying to say onto a screen. In these patients, the scientists monitored activity from neurons in Wernicke's area with electrodes and were able to decode what the participants were attempting to communicate.

Silva said these discoveries rewrite the textbook on Wernicke's area. Adeen Flinker, a neuroscientist at New York University who was not involved in the study, agreed.

"We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why," Flinker told Live Science.

The new findings could lead to better brain-computer interfaces for treating aphasia, Silva said. Until now, patients who have benefited from these interfaces have mainly had problems with the pathways linking their motor cortex and mouth muscles, he said, such as people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

"This is actually a small number of patients relative to the number of patients that have aphasia ‪—‬ so a language disorder from injury to the cortex itself," Silva said. These patients have vocal paralysis but are unable to benefit from BCIs because of this cortical damage, Flinker noted.

This special spot in Wernicke's area could be a new target for brain-computer interfaces aimed at helping patients with aphasia, Silva continued. "We really think that this is an area that could expand the number of people that could benefit from the technology in the near future," he concluded.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Silva, A. B., Leonard, M. K., Hullett, P. W., Levy, D. F., Wang, C., Xu, D., Bhaya-Grossman, I., & Chang, E. F. (2026). A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke's area. Science, 394(6826). https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef8963

#6459. The Safest Way to Handle a Kitchen Grease Fire

A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you. Here's how to handle one safely.

One of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it. So much of cooking depends on knowing how far we can push the heat—getting a pan hot enough to sear steak or bringing oil just to the right temperature for a batch of fried chicken. I’ve yet to lose the little thrill of flambéing a steak au poivre or a rum-laced bananas Foster, but after years in kitchens, I have a healthy respect for high heat.

That respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and Christmas Eve are the three peak days of the year for home cooking fires.

What makes a grease fire especially dangerous is that many of the things we’d instinctively do to put out a fire can actually cause it to spread. Fortunately, handling a grease fire safely is a fairly simple matter of knowing what to reach for and what to leave alone.

Whether you’re sauteing vegetables in a little olive oil or frying chicken in a Dutch oven, it’s important to recognize when your cooking fat is getting too hot. Different oils have different smoke points (the temperatures at which they begin to smoke) but if an oil continues to heat well beyond that point, it can eventually ignite without ever coming into direct contact with a flame. Overheating isn’t the only culprit, though. Oil that splashes onto a hot burner or an open flame can also catch fire, as can grease that has accumulated around the burners.

I find a thermometer invaluable when I’m deep-frying, but it’s important to keep an eye on the pan even when sauteing. It’s frighteningly easy to get distracted chopping the next ingredient or chatting with your dinner guests. If you notice smoke rising from your pan, turn off the burner immediately.

Should the oil catch fire, leave the pan where it is. As instinctive as it may be to move it to the sink, carrying burning oil through the kitchen is a serious burn hazard, and risks spreading the fire.

The most important thing to remember about a grease fire is that water will only make it worse. Most of us are familiar with the rather unpleasant sensation of hot oil spattering onto our hands when moisture finds its way into a sizzling pan. The science behind that reaction is the same here: Water sinks and turns rapidly to steam, agitating the oil. When the oil is burning, that sudden expansion can send flames and droplets of burning oil well beyond the stovetop.

A fire extinguisher may seem like the obvious thing to reach for, but not all extinguishers are suited for grease fires. Class K extinguishers are designed specifically for fires involving cooking oils and fats, and they can be useful if you have one and know how to use it safely. For a small grease fire contained within a pan, though, there’s a simpler (and considerably less expensive) piece of kitchen equipment that can do the job: a metal lid.

Both the NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration recommend keeping one nearby when cooking. A small, contained grease fire can often be extinguished simply by depriving it of oxygen. Provided the flames haven’t spread beyond the pan, and you can approach it safely, here’s what to do:

If covering the pan doesn’t extinguish the flames, it’s important to recognize that the situation is beyond your control. Get everyone outside and call 911.

#6458. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

#6457. McDonald’s Is Reportedly Testing A Major Chicken Menu Overhaul—Here’s What We Know

The Golden Arches might be coming for the Colonel.

McDonald’s has been paying close attention to its chicken menu lately. Between the return of the Snack Wrap, the introduction of McCrispy Strips, and several new dipping sauces, it’s clear the chain is looking to become a bigger player in the fast-food chicken game. If the latest reports are true, some of its biggest changes might still be ahead.

McDonald’s is reportedly testing five hand-breaded chicken menu items in select U.S. markets, including Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the Tucson, Arizona, area. The information comes from McFranchisee, an account on X that regularly shares details about the chain’s operations and upcoming menu changes.

The biggest difference with this potential menu overhaul is how the chicken would be prepared. Rather than simply introducing new flavors or sauces, McDonald’s is reportedly experimenting with having employees bread the chicken by hand inside its restaurants.

Among the alleged test items is a new McSpicy chicken sandwich. According to the report, all five items are also available as meals, with prices ranging from $8.19 to $9.99 at the location pictured in the social media post.

A similar test is also taking place in Ireland.

I’m particularly interested in how hand-breading could change the texture of McDonald’s chicken. Having taste-tested plenty of fast-food chicken sandwiches and tenders, I’ve found that the breading can make or break the entire experience. A crispier, more substantial coating could make McDonald’s a much stronger competitor to chains like Popeyes and Chick-fil-A.

Rolling out hand-breaded chicken across thousands of restaurants, however, is easier said than done.

The reported tests are designed to evaluate customer demand, preparation costs, and how the additional steps could affect kitchen operations. Some franchisees have reportedly expressed concerns about increased labor requirements and potential kitchen renovations.

While McDonald’s hasn’t officially confirmed the five-item lineup or specific U.S. test locations, the idea of hand-breaded chicken isn’t entirely out of left field.

During its November earnings call, the company confirmed that it had begun setting up operational pilots for hand-breaded chicken in the U.S. and Ireland. It also announced plans for larger U.S. sales tests at roughly 100 restaurants in early 2027.

For now, there’s no confirmed nationwide U.S. release date or guarantee that all five reported items will make it onto the permanent menu.
